utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning to everybody. Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-14-A, the Prosecution versus Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Can everybody hear me? I think it's the case. So we can resume our hearing. We will continue with the submissions of the Prosecution. I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to my learned colleagues. I will continue with my submissions from yesterday, and we'll deal with certain factual matters that arise on the basis of the additional evidence. After I'm finished, and I will be looking at the -- responding, I'm sorry, to the appellant's submissions regarding Ahmici and Stari Vitez specifically. Then there will be two more counsel who will make submissions on behalf of the Prosecution. Ms. Howick will follow me and then after that will be Ms. Jarvis. If I could start -- yesterday I left off by showing you two documents. Those two documents were the 12th and the 13th exhibit to the appellant's fourth additional evidence motion. I just want to clarify, in fact correct one thing. I think in my attempt yesterday to present my submissions on both of them to you, just before the end of the day I got them actually reversed and out of order. I had indicated that document number 13 was the later of the two orders, document 12 was the first order and document 13 followed. Actually, they are reversed, if I understand it correctly. Document 13 is the prior order, and it appears to be an order from the 7th Muslim Brigade, which is a subordinate unit of the 3rd Corps, and it indicates -- it's dated April 16th and it indicates that the Muslim forces had been attacked and that the 7th Muslim Brigade was being sent to reach the village of Ahmici as soon as possible to join in the combat operations. I had erroneously indicated that the -- this was the second of the two, after looking at it again last night. This is the first order, then document 12 is the second order, which is on the 17th, just so that there's no confusion. And the document 13 indicates at some point on the 16th that the 7th Muslim Brigade was sent to join in the defence of the attack and in the combat operations in Ahmici. It's my understanding that this was put in by the Defence to indicate that there was combat in Ahmici on the 16th. I think we already know from BA5 that the Territorial Defence in Ahmici was engaged in an attack and he indicated, as my friend acknowledged, that there were some members of the Territorial Defence in Ahmici. He described they were defending it with hunting rifles. Yesterday, in his submissions, if I understand them correctly, my learned colleague indicated that the Trial Chamber from paragraphs 407 to 410, had accepted that there was no evidence that the BH army or other armed Muslim resistance was in Ahmici. Simply -- and I think he probably relies on these documents to indicate to the contrary that there was an armed resistance in Ahmici. I just asked you, in response to that comment, to review the Trial Chamber's judgement at 407 to 410, as in my respectful submission that's not what the Trial Chamber finds. It acknowledges that there was a Territorial Defence in Ahmici, and it cites the evidence for the proposition that there was no military justification to attack Ahmici, not to say that there wasn't, in fact, Territorial Defence in Ahmici. Having clarified that matter, I'd like to move on to my submissions relating to the attack on Ahmici and respond to some of the submissions made by Mr. Hayman. One of the major issues that was raised by the appellant was whether or not the military police were under the command of Blaskic on the morning of the 16th, when the attack started, at 5.30 in the morning. The Prosecution asks that you, when considering this issue, you keep it in the context of the rest of the evidence. When my learned colleague referred to my submissions from a year ago last November about this case is not about Ahmici, I stand by those submissions. This case is about an attack in a number of municipalities, in approximately 20 villages, from the 16th onwards, and it's a coordinated, planned, and orchestrated attack, and the Trial Chamber was completely correct in referring to this to determine whether or not the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone was involved. Now, the appellant indicates that the military police were not attached to him at the relevant time. What we do know from the trial record is on the 15th of April, at 3.00 in the afternoon, the chief of the General Staff issued an order attaching the military police and the Vitezovi to the appellant. The appellant indicates that was -- they were attached in the event of an attack, and until an attack, they were not attached to him for combat operations. He claims that they were attached to him on April 16th, at 11.45. According to him, this is when the military police themselves actually attached themselves to him. It's because at that point in time the appellant claims that Ljubicic contacts him because the HVO are under attack in Ahmici. Now, it's important to consider this in the context of his evidence. Once again, the dependency is that the HVO attack Ahmici. I'm sorry, the ABiH attack Ahmici. Once the HVO is under attack by the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the military police, I presume, contact him at 11.42 to tell them, "We're engaged in combat operations and we would like to attach ourselves to the Central Bosnia operative zone." It's this dependency on the HVO being the victims of an attack by the Bosnian government which, once again, in my submission, cannot be at all substantiated on the facts. So according to the appellant, despite the fact that he received an order from the chief of staff that they were to attach themselves in the event of attack, despite the fact that he was the commander of the zone, and despite the fact that he claims he was woken at 5.00 a.m. by his chief of staff and told that there was an attack, it's not until over sixth and a half hours later that the subordinate unit, the military police, tell him when they're going to attach themselves to him. Now, we know, based on document P12 -- P12 is a document we now have before us and P12 is the document that was issued, at least the date on the order is 1.30 in the morning on the morning of the 16th. On the morning of the 16th, at 1.30 in the morning, we now have an order from Blaskic to the head of the military police. Now, why would Blaskic issue a combat order at 1.30 in the morning to the military police if they're not attached to him yet? And it is a combat order. It's tasking for combat purposes, and it talks of repelling their attack during your counter-attack. It then speaks in this order, at 1.30 in the morning, to the military police: "Strong enemy forces are in front of you, and forces of the Zrinski Brigade are to your right, and the HVO Vitez is to your left." The time of readiness is 5.30 in the morning on April 16th, the exact time as the attack started. What did the appellant, Blaskic, testify to about issuing this order? This order we now have before us as PA12, the order to the military police? Blaskic testified at trial that he never issued any written orders to the military police that evening, prior to the combat operations. You heard yesterday of the three orders that he did say he issued. They were Defence Exhibits 267, 268, and 269. These were the orders that were presented on the evening -- the 15th. Now, during his testimony on the 8th of March, Colonel Blaskic says, in response to a question by Mr. Nobilo. “Q. Apart from these orders, did you issue to the military police, on 15 April 1993, any other orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.” Why is it that he would indicate at trial that he didn't issue any other orders to the military police and that he didn't issue any orders other than the three that were noted? Is it possible because the order actually could have been construed by the Trial Chamber as a combat order to the military police at a time when he claims that they weren't attached to him for that purpose? We also know on the record that on the 15th of April, in the afternoon - and it's reflected in the war diary - that the appellant met with the commander of the 4th Military Police, Pasko Ljubicic, at approximately 5.00 in the afternoon. He met with him at the same time as the Vitezovi commander, the commander of the Tvrtko 2, which is a special purposes unit. In his testimony, he acknowledges that he spoke with them at that time and explained to them and issued the orders, I think it was 267 and 268, orally. Those orders actually hadn't been sent, and he issued those orders orally to them at the time. If I could just -- I'd like to refer to the testimony of one of the witnesses. If I could just go into private session for a minute or two, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we'll move to what the appellant said about the Vitez Brigade, and their involvement. Now, in response to a question by Judge Shahabuddeen at the trial, Blaskic answered to Judge Shahabuddeen:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vitez Brigade did not get any tasks from me in the area of Ahmici, nor, to the best of my knowledge, the commander of the Vitez Brigade. Now, I'd like to refer to Prosecution rebuttal Exhibits 6, 7, 8, and 10, which, in my submission, clearly show that when the appellant said that the Vitez Brigade did not get any tasks from me in the area of Ahmici, nor did the commander of the Vitez Brigade, that it was clearly false. I've asked that Prosecution rebuttal Exhibit 6 be put before you, and I understand if you go to the computer evidence button, it should appear on your screen, Your Honours. Now, you'll see that this is at 10.00 in the morning of April the 16th. I've tried to highlight or sidebar, I guess, the passage. If it's legible. This is on April 16th, at 10.00 in the morning, and it's a report on the situation in the area of responsibility. Now, you'll see that the first line says: "Pursuant to your order number" - and that order number is a sequence of numbers coming from Colonel Blaskic - "of April 16th, we inform you of the following." Therefore, this is not a random report on his area of responsibility. He's responding to a request before 10.00 a.m., from Colonel Blaskic, to report on the situation. So this isn't the first contact, clearly. There's a previous contact at some point in time; we don't know when. And then in the report, in the second highlighted passage - I'll see if I can just get it enlarged - it says: "Our units are advancing on Donja Veceriska, whose fall is imminent, and in Ahmici." Now, the appellant has argued that this is simply a report in the area of responsibility and that our forces mean all forces in the area. Why would the commander of the Vitez Brigade be giving a report about Ahmici when his forces are not there? And when the forces that are there are the 4th Military Police, who are not attached to him yet? If I could go to Prosecution Exhibit 7. I'll just commence until the document can come up on the screen. This is a document dated April 16th, at 10.35. It should be coming up now on screen. The document at 10.35 is from Colonel Blaskic to the commander of the Vitez Brigade. The subject is engagement in further combat operations, and it refers to activities which are to be done in connection with the report of the commander of the Vitez Brigade and the number listed is 02125-1093. This is the order number of the previous document I just showed you, PA6. So this is a response to Cerkez's report on the situation. The order says: "The following shall be done in connection with your previous report." And then it says: Capture a number of villages, and one of them is Ahmici, and the order is that they be captured completely at 10.35 in the morning. The appellant has not explained in his testimony why he would be issuing an order to the Vitez Brigade to capture Ahmici completely when he hasn't even been informed by Pasko Ljubicic at 11.42 that the military police wish to be subordinated to him because of the events in Ahmici. If I can go to Prosecution rebuttal document 8, please. This is a document from April 16th, and we know by the ordering numbers that this document is sometime before 2.00 in the afternoon on April 16th. It's a report regarding undertaking further combat operations at sometime before 2.00, and the commander of the Vitez Brigade reports back that the village of Ahmici is 70 per cent done. This is in relation to combat operations in Ahmici by the Vitez Brigade. If I can now turn to the last one, number 10. Now, this is a document dated April 16th, at 2.00 in the afternoon. In the first paragraph in this order or report from Colonel Blaskic to the commander of the Vitez Brigade, Mario Cerkez, it says: "Regarding your report number 02-25-12/93." That's the order number of the document I just showed you as PA8, and it's the order number of the document in which Cerkez is reporting back that Ahmici is 70 per cent done. That's the document that's referred to by its order number. And in this document, which is at 2.00 in the afternoon, at paragraph 2, it says: "Continue the activities described in article 1 of your report." Well, article 1 of the previous report includes the fact that the village of Ahmici is 70 per cent done and that the Vitez Brigade has arrested 14 men, who are accommodated in weekend houses in Nadioci. When considering the involvement of both the Vitez Brigade and the military police in Ahmici, and very importantly, the involvement of Dario Kordic, I'd ask that you take note of the war diary. The appellant's logbook or war diary, which he submitted as his exhibit. On the 16th of April, there are 13 contacts in the space of about 11 hours, 10 hours, between Blaskic and Dario Kordic, and there are eight contacts or references from Pasko Ljubicic to the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. In light of this evidence, and in light of the evidence at trial, I submit that it's clearly not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to have found that the order D269, which was admitted at trial - this is the order at 1.30 in the morning to the commander of the Vitez Brigade, Mario Cerkez - it's not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to have found in the circumstances that that was a combat order. If I could now move to a few issues that were raised by the learned counsel for the appellant regarding his submissions in Ahmici, and I'd just like to comment on a few of them. First of all, the appellants relied on the first exhibit to the second Rule 115 motion, and that's the ministry of the interior report, and it's called the MUP report. And it's been relied on extensively in the written submissions and was referred to yesterday by the appellant, because that document describes a meeting on the night of the 15th at Dario Kordic's house. That's the only document we have before you, and we haven't -- and all it is is an investigative report, which, if I recall, is many years after the fact. And there's just one thing I wish to bring to your attention, and it's included in the submissions in any event, but when you're considering this investigations report years later, note that the report is partially based on the information provided to the Ministry of the Interior investigators from counsel for Blaskic. Now, this is a report after he was convicted. And in the appellant's reply brief, in support of their second motion to admit additional evidence, registry pages 13897, there's a recognition that the MUP report appears to incorporate information the investigators obtained from interviewing Mr. Nobilo. With respect, unless the underlying evidence is brought forward, this report is of little evidentiary value. The appellant also relies on the MUP report to point out that there was an individual named Cicko who was involved in this crime, and the appellant testified at trial that he was a criminal and that he's the type of person that was engaged in this. You heard testimony from one of the witnesses last week who referred to this individual as well. Now, the MUP report refers to this individual Cicko as Miroslav Bralo. Now, I won't place the evidence before you, but I'll tell you where to find it, if you're so interested. This was referred to by Mr. Harmon last week. Which is that at OTP Exhibits 188 to 191 - these documents are under seal, so I won't place them or go into the documents themselves - but there was the creation of the Alfa Force, and the commander was an individual named Kris, Kris with a K, and Cicko was the deputy commander. Now, you heard evidence last week from a witness who talked about the presence of this Cicko at the -- at a meeting on the night of the 15th, in preparation of the attack. Colonel Blaskic's testimony, at T20139, was that he thought that Miroslav Bralo, or Cicko, was actually in prison for murder on April 16th, and he testified that Cicko was a deranged person. Colonel Blaskic also testified that he received information on the 25th of May, 1993, that this individual was one of the perpetrators in Ahmici. He further testified: "If a name like that existed, then I'm certain that steps to remove him from the HVO" would have been taken. Eight days later, after receiving this information on May 25th, 1993 that Cicko was a perpetrator in Ahmici, Blaskic was informed, if you look at Prosecution Exhibit PA34, it's a report from Mario Cerkez that -- as to activities, and at the end of the report, it says that Cicko was used in military operations, and the report also indicates that operations took place along with the Jokers, the Vitezovi, and the Vitez Brigade. Lastly, this same Cicko that the appellant are pointing the finger at and relying on in the MUP report is referred to in the Trial Chamber's judgement at paragraph 472. At the end of paragraph 472, the last sentence, the Court indicates that: Witness A, who is a witness who testified in closed session, Witness A said that he heard a person named Cicko speak in these terms with regard to the events of April 16th: "Everyone is washing their hands now as regards Ahmici, but we all know that Blaskic has ordered that no prisoners of war were of interest to him; only dead bodies." It's the same Cicko that he's receiving a report on on July 2nd who he, as the evidence at trial indicates, he was aware of in the Alfa Force prior to this, and the year wasn't in 1993 and who is now being blamed in the MUP report for the events. Now, the Defence have argued in their appeal brief that the Court could not rely on this piece of evidence because it was hearsay from Witness 2, without getting into a full argument, it's Prosecution's submission that hearsay is clearly admissible, and certainly Witness 2's hearsay evidence was certainly something that the Trial Chamber could rely on, much more so than a MUP report. At least Witness 2 was present to be cross-examined. Sorry. I indicated that Witness A, not Witness 2. Sorry. Yesterday my learned colleague indicated that the British Battalion, when they went to Ahmici, did not see any massacre or comparable activity. Now, I take it, though I may be wrong, but I take it that this is the reference to when the British Battalion went with one of the witnesses who testified last week to Ahmici in an armoured personnel carrier, or Warrior. Now, as you know from the witness's evidence, I won't go into the evidence, but you'll know from the evidence where the location of that witness was, and that witness was not actually in the centre of Ahmici in the sense of the area where the MOS was and wasn't permitted to go any further than the area that he located. A British army officer who testified on the 20th November 1997 indicated that he was in an armoured personnel carrier on the afternoon of April 16th. It's impossible to tell from his testimony whether he was in the armoured personnel carrier with BA3 or whether he was separate. It's not clear. But he indicates that in the time that he drove around in the early afternoon of April 16th, that he could see civilian houses on fire, houses destroyed, bodies and civilians that ran up, I think a total number of 13 that climbed into the back of his armoured personnel carrier to be taken to safety. You'll recall the position of BA3, and he indicates that he only found out 10 to 15 days later. This is conveniently the exact time period that the appellant put forward as an approximately time period when he found out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a situation report as of 2000 hours, so approximately 8.00. On the fourth page of this report, it talks about the -- I'm sorry. On the screen, I've only been able to get a part of it, but it talks about relations with the HVO, and it indicates in the line above it that in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, the HVO units are attacking the Muslim population and the units of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, accepting that this document is a document from the 18th of April, 1993, from the command of the 3rd Corps of the Bosnian army, I would respectfully submit that BA3 either knew or was in a position to know, as of the night of the 17th or the morning of the 18th, as to what happened in Ahmici, not ten to 15 days later, or if he did, it's certainly inconsistent with the knowledge of the command. Another point raised in the appellant's submissions was the video clip they showed from Mr. Martin Bell at a press conference on the 27th of April. This was 11 days after the crimes were committed in Ahmici. It's important to note that both Kordic and Valenta, the two extremists, according to the appellant, were both present at the press conference, and they were there when there was an agreement on behalf of the HVO to initiate an investigation. In cross-examination, Mr. Bell acknowledged that the actual reporting prior to April 27th, including his reporting, drew attention to the HVO in the area and had a global effect on the HVO. He acknowledged that news reports were bringing pressure on Croatia and that they were embarrassed by the situation and the pressure. He indicated as well that he was aware that Margaret Thatcher actually cancelled the trip to Croatia at that time. An exhibit, OTP Exhibit 532, which is a report, was submitted to Mr. Bell, in which Mate Boban, who was the president of the HB-HZ and the supreme commander of the HVO, had said that due to Ahmici, EU ministers have almost announced sanctions against Croatia. He acknowledged that the pressure being brought to bear on Croatia was actually a matter of concern for the HVO. It's respectfully submitted that when Blaskic, Kordic, and Valenta were at this press conference on April 27th, and when Blaskic spoke, it's hard to imagine that he would have said something in front of this press conference in light of this international pressure other than he was horrified by it and that something would take place, an investigation. And I'll come back later to comments which Colonel Blaskic made after this press conference about Ahmici and ask that you keep those in mind when you're looking at Martin Bell's testimony. In concluding my submissions on Prosecution's response to the submissions by Mr. Hayman, my learned colleague, I'll just ask you to take note of the additional evidence which is filed. I think Mr. Hayman did a good job of trying to reconcile the additional evidence that the appellants have put forward, but despite his eloquence, I submit they can't be reconciled. If you look at Exhibit 1, the first document put forward in the second motion upon which the appellant relies to indicate that Blaskic is not responsible for Ahmici, it indicates that certain members of the forces on the ground, enraged by the death of their comrades, took revenge; indicates these are essentially rogue elements in an unplanned operation on the 16th. Exhibit 4 doesn't give any indication as to what happened, doesn't indicate that they were rogue elements acting out of revenge, but simply just states that Kordic and Kostroman are responsible. Now, these two documents are from the intelligence sources, and the dates on the front of the document's cover are February 1994 and March 1994. Exhibit 13 says that the Jokers revolted because three of their members were killed. Once again, this is an explanation of revenge, not that it was planned. I'd ask that you keep in mind the appellant's testimony himself when he indicates that this event in Ahmici had to be planned. If the appellant's submission is that the events in Ahmici had to be planned -- and this is his testimony. His testimony is that at trial, and only at trial, interestingly, the appellant indicates that he realised after hearing the evidence at trial that in fact the Bungalow had not been attacked that morning. At trial, that's when he first realised it, when he heard evidence of witnesses who appeared. He also acknowledged that this event would have had to have been planned and orchestrated, and planned by someone higher than the commander of the 4th Military Battalion. Well, how is he relying on documents now, months after the attack, which indicates that it was a revolt, that it was a revenge? His own testimony refutes the very documents that he's relying on. Exhibit 14, which is the one that indicates that Mr. Cerkez is a coward by nature, and therefore would not be involved, seems to be directly refuted by the very documents that were signed by Colonel Blaskic himself. And as well, Exhibit 14 refers to the crimes in Ahmici as a revenge to the killing of HVO soldiers and the capturing of their commander. Once again, this isn't, first of all, what happened in fact, and it's certainly not what's relied upon by the appellant now, in light of BA2's testimony. The MUP report gives a completely different version than the other reports relied upon by the appellant, and it indicates that the crime in Ahmici was planned, orchestrated, and ordered by political figures, while at trial the appellant indicates that the crimes were committed by the military police from higher orders, but he himself could not say that it was Kordic. With respect, it's unclear which of these the appellant is actually relying on. It's a little bit of anyone but me defence. And it sets forward positions which are inconsistent among themselves and inconsistent with some of the appellant's own testimony at trial. With respect, this evidence, inconsistent amongst itself, certainly is not something that would even cause the Trial Chamber reasonable doubt, and it certainly isn't anything by which this Appeals Chamber, on the standard, could conclude that no reasonable Trial Chamber on the evidence before it could have convicted. Those are my submissions in relation to Ahmici. I will now move to submissions on Stari Vitez. In light of the fact that I'd hoped to finish within an hour to an hour and 15 minutes to allow us to finish on time today and allow my colleagues -- what I will refer you to is certain documents in relation to Stari Vitez, which in the Prosecution's submission show that the Vitezovi were acting under the command and control of the appellant. My colleague Ms. Jarvis will make submissions on one aspect of Stari Vitez, but I'll try and limit my submissions on Stari Vitez to the documents I'd like to refer you to, and these are additional evidence documents. You'll recall that the attack on Stari Vitez was on April 16th, the same time as the attack on Ahmici. It was against the Muslim population. It was planned and well organised. It's the conclusion that HVO troops, including HVO regular troops - and there was testimony last week to that effect - participated in the attack on Stari Vitez and that the Muslim civilian population was targeted, as found by the Trial Chamber, paragraph 507. It's also important to remember that the headquarters of Colonel Blaskic was only 300 metres away from Stari Vitez. There's -- I think it's Exhibit 79 at trial, it's called the distance project, and in it, you can see, if you look at it, that the area is extremely small. Blaskic's headquarters is 300 metres from Stari Vitez. That Mario Cerkez's headquarters, as indicated by a witness last week, is less than -- I think it's a hundred metres, I think he even said 50 metres from the headquarters. This is where hundreds of people were detained afterwards. I think if you look at the exhibit as well, you'll see that Ahmici is something like six minutes by car from Blaskic's headquarters. Now, in relation to the attack, we have the submissions of the appellant, which I won't go through, but which indicate that the HVO was attacked by the Muslim forces on the morning of the 16th, that in an answer to a question by Judge Rodrigues, he expressed his view publicly that they cannot undertake any operations whatever on Stari Vitez because of the need to guarantee the security and safety of the population in Stari Vitez, and that was in relation -- his comments were in relation to, as I recall, the July 18th attack. He also indicates that he did not approve or receive a request to use artillery on the morning of the 16th of April, but you'll also note that the record indicates there was artillery and Blaskic himself testified that he controlled the use of artillery. I'm just asking for an exhibit to be brought on the screen. Now, you'll recall that the Defence has indicated, in paragraph 514 of the judgement, was that in relation to the attacks on April - specifically, I think, that's in reference to April 18th - the defence was that the Vitezovi alone committed the crimes, and the Vitezovi refused to recognise the relationship of subordination to Blaskic. It was referred to by the Trial Chamber as the defence at trial. Now, the first document I just want to bring to your attention is the 20th of January, 1993. It's the subordination of the Vitezovi to Colonel Blaskic at the time. Now, this is in January 1993, long before. Then I would like to refer to Prosecution appeal rebuttal Exhibit 24. This is a report sent by the commander of the Vitezovi on the 15th of April, 1993. It's a protest to the Bosnian army about the treatment of some of its members. And at the very end, it states: "Our unit will continue to carry out all orders issued by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic and to be in the single system of command and control." This is on the 15th of April. Now, the appellant has noted that it's not sent to Blaskic. This very document is not sent to Blaskic. As you may recall from the testimony of a superior officer in the HVO, his testimony was that it wasn't necessary, that it wasn't irregular and wasn't outside the chain of command if the units informed the Main Staff of their operations. And it would seem a little bit odd that they're indicating that they're carrying out the operations and orders issued by Colonel Blaskic, if the Defence would rely on the fact that it wasn't sent to him to refute that. Now I refer to Prosecution Exhibit 37. This is a commendation by Colonel Blaskic to the Vitezovi for the role in "... defending our territories and common interests of the Croatian people." It says: "Your role is great." He commends the soldiers of the special-purpose unit, the Vitezovi, on April 18th, 1993, shortly after the attacks on the 16th of April on Stari Vitez and the attacks of 18th of April on Stari Vitez. If I can now refer you to Prosecution Exhibit 25. You'll recall the testimony of the appellant's witnesses about the need for command and control and reporting, though there might be communications, there's not necessarily control; though there might be command, you would have to look for things such as reporting to determine whether or not there was actually the evidence of control. This is a report by the commander of the Vitezovi on April 26th, 1993. Now, if I could just refer to -- the top of the document reads: "In the treacherous enemy attack by the army of BH..." Once again it appears that the-- I'm sorry. Let me begin again. "In the treacherous enemy attack by the army of BH," in other words the Muslim forces, "on everything that is Croatian, on orders from the commander of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, I carried out the following combat operations." Now, if you look down the list, it's from April 16th to April 25th. You'll also recall that the crimes committed in Vitez and Stari Vitez were on April 16th and April 18th, and the crimes committed in Gacice were found by the Trial Chamber to have finished on the 20th. The Defence at trial was that the Vitezovi did not report to Blaskic and would not subordinate themselves to Blaskic for combat activities. On April 16th, it lists that at 5.00 in the morning - this is the same time as the attack orders, not defensive orders - Stari Vitez, that's Old Vitez, they conduct an operation there, fighting is still in progress. They refer to the village of Novaci and that the centre of town is cleared. I note that they use the word "cleared." They don't use the word "ethnically cleansed" in their report to Blaskic as to their operations on the 16th. And the testimony at trial is that, for example, the Trial Chamber's findings at paragraph 499, in relation to the 18th of April is that -- and I'll just ask you to refer down to the 18th of April in the report. It says: Village of Novaci cleared. Novaci is an area in the town of Vitez, and you're aware of the fact that there were crimes committed at this time. If you look at the 16th of April, the 18th of April, and the reference in the 19th of April to Gacice, each one of them uses the word "cleared." The evidence at trial was that it wasn't a military operation. And in fact, the Defence doesn't claim that the Vitezovi conducted exclusively military operations. They claimed at trial that the Vitezovi committed the crimes but were not under Blaskic's subordination. Now, in relation to the report on April 18th that they were operating in the area of Vitez, Stari Vitez, I won't take you to it, but in the war diary on April 18th, Blaskic calls the commander of the Vitezovi at 1408 and indicates that artillery support is on its way. At 1755, approximately 6.00 in the evening of the 18th, the war diary indicates that Kraljevic, the commander of the Vitezovi, came to see Blaskic to report on the operation and that one of his soldiers had been killed. Why is he coming to report to Blaskic on the 18th when he refuses to subordinate himself to him? Why does he feel the need to tell him that a soldier has been killed? Blaskic indicates he has no relationship with the Vitezovi during this relevant time. The reporting orally on the 18th to Blaskic, as indicated in the war diary, and this written report indicating that they're acting under the combat orders of Colonel Blaskic refute any claim that the Vitezovi were not operating pursuant to command and control of Colonel Blaskic. There's a number of references in the war diary to operations that take place, and I simply note them because the Defence has indicated that it's important to see whether there's reporting back to determine control. For example, on April 25th, at 2125 in the war diary, Blaskic orders the commander of the Vitezovi to send 20 men to Busovaca. That's in the war diary. On the evening of the 25th, that Blaskic orders Kraljevic to send 20 men to Busovaca. If you look on the report on April 25th, 1993, when they report -- they're reporting on April 26th as to the operations that conducted -- took place by the Vitezovi in the days previously. Reporting on April 25th, they indicate that they restored the line on the Kuber elevation and Busovaca, my understanding is SO means municipality, fighting in progress. It's consistent with the war diary at 2125, when Blaskic orders Kraljevic to send 20 men to Busovaca. The next exhibit, though I won't put it up on screen, is the 456/32. This is on May 7th, 1993. It's been referred to already, but it's the report by Blaskic to the supreme commanders of the armed forces in Mostar, and he indicates, as has already been put before you, that command and control function properly, and all missions proceed in a planned fashion, according to orders, with detailed knowledge of the situation, full coordination and control. There's no reason for Blaskic not to tell his subordinates if he has problems with the units who are under his control. And this report on May 7th, it lists the Vitezovi as part of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone HVO forces. Now, there's a passage in this document which was referred to in cross-examination by my learned colleague in cross-examination that there was some difficulty with the battalion in Fojnica, and it was put to one of the witnesses that, well, this must demonstrate that there's problems of command and control. It indicates in the document that all units are carrying out their task except for the battalion in Fojnica, who are taking a neutral position vis-a-vis the Muslims. First of all, the report doesn't refer to any of the units that are committing crimes. What it refers to is a commander in Fojnica who refuses to attack the Muslims. And you'll see, in relation to - and I can take you through them if you wish - to a number of exhibits at trial, exhibits at trial which range from Prosecution Exhibit 456/45 to 456/54, would indicate that the commander of the Fojnica Brigade refuses to comply with an order to attack the Muslims, as he indicates that there's no conflict with the Muslims in the area. In fact, there's a statement by the Muslim and Croat community leaders in Fojnica - this is OTP Exhibit 491 - where they complained about their replacement of the commander, this is the replacement of the commander by Blaskic, because the previous commander had maintained peace and a common existence between the Croatian and Muslim people. It's just quite telling that the one problem that he reports as to commanders is someone who won't follow his orders to attack Muslims, not the ones who do and commit crimes. And lastly, I'll refer to Prosecution Exhibit 38. I think it should be up on your screen in computer evidence. This is dated June 1993 and it's a report once again to the head of the Croatian community. It's a report to the Defence department, and it's a report to Blaskic's superior, the chief of the Croatian Defence Council, Major General Petkovic. Now, what's happening at this time is that the Croatian Defence Council is considering reforming the Vitezovi and actually incorporating them into a regiment, into the Bruno Busic regiment. And does Blaskic then indicate in the report in June 1992 that it would be a very good idea that their rogue unit, operating solely under Kraljevic, taking no responsibility for Blaskic's orders, and that he's been attempting for a long time to have the Vitezovi reformulated into a different unit under his command? Let's just see what the document reads. The first paragraph says: "Today, I received the commander of the Vitezovi and members of its command, who expressed their unhappiness with the insulting words used in relation to the behaviour of the Vitezovi soldiers" - it refers to some comments - "and with the order abolishing the Independent Battalion Vitezovi PPN and incorporating it into the Bruno Busic regiment." It then goes on to state that he can understand the intentions of the head of the Croatian Defence Council and the defence department, but commends the Vitezovi by indicating that the Vitezovi Battalion has in fact performed all its assigned combat tasks, that is a real guarantee of tenacity, security, and professionalism, and that in current combat operations especially, it inspires stability and solid morale in all soldiers on the front lines. On the next page of the document, it says: "I know that the unit is made up of young men who sometimes kick over the traces a little." I'm not sure if this is an expression of what the problems are with the Vitezovi, but if it is, it certainly indicates he's not very concerned. "But I know that the unit command is on top of the situation and has absolute control over the entire formation of this unit, and that all Central Bosnia Operative Zone commands are carried out in their entirety, without question and on time. "I make the following requests to you personally, sir, the head of the HZ-HB defence department, and you, sir, the chief of the HVO. "1, that the order to reform the Vitezovi be temporarily revoked." With respect, Colonel Blaskic is not complaining about the Vitezovi, he's not concerned about their criminal activity, he's not indicating to his superiors that they have to be re-subordinated in different units, he's not taking steps against the Vitezovi. He's using the Vitezovi, they're reporting to him, and he's indicating that they are following all of his tasks in their entirety, without question and on time. Now, this report, June of 1993, is after the report that the Defence relies on. You'll recall that the Defence have put before you a document where the Vitezovi have taken over a petrol station. It was referred to in their submissions yesterday. And that after having taken over a petrol station, they then refused to report to Blaskic and Blaskic has to -- there's a document indicating that Blaskic has to contact the Main Staff in Mostar and have them re-subordinated again around May 9th. I won't go into the documents, but if you refer to Prosecution Exhibit 41, it's a Security and Information Service report on the Kalen petrol station in Vitezovi. What it actually indicates in this report is that the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, that's Blaskic, came to the conclusion that the Kalen petrol station should be captured and thereby saved from destruction because the tanks were full of fuel. This task was entrusted to Kraljevic. Three members of his unit were killed. And upon implementing the order, Kraljevic gave the petrol station over to Colonel Blaskic, that is, to the logistics of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Then there is a dispute by the civilian authorities as to who is going to operate the petrol station and whether or not the Vitezovi, and by inference, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, can keep its proceeds. The dispute results in a rebellion, according to this report, from some members of the Vitezovi and that he then seeks the intervention by the command in Mostar. Now, it's true that the command indicate an order back that they're to be subordinate, and that document is before you. It appears, though, that this matter that is of grave concern doesn't relate to combat activities; it relates to what appears to be is a dispute between the civilian authorities and the military. And when you look at this operation which was in April, and the request -- the re-subordination in May, keep in mind the report shortly thereafter, I think about one month after, on June 22nd, where Blaskic reports that they follow his command. In my submission, he's referring to combat operations. When you look at all these documents together and the operations that took place and the Defence position that the Vitezovi committed crimes but they just weren't subordinated to him, I think it's not necessary that it's proven beyond a reasonable doubt at this stage that that's the case. All that you have to determine on the basis of the additional evidence is whether or not the Trial Chamber's findings were reasonable. There's just two other matters I want to refer to and then I'll try and finish before the break and hand the Prosecution's remaining submission to others. The first, it's an interesting issue raised originally in the cross-examination of some of the witnesses and then followed up by His Honour Judge Schomburg, and it's the use of the language "mop-up." The appellant relies on three witnesses from last week, BA1, BA3, and Mr. Watkins for an explanation that the term "mop-up" is a standard military term used for legitimate military operations and to rebut the Trial Chamber's findings in paragraph 646, concluding that the language in Trial Exhibit 300 had the connotations of eradication. I would respectfully submit that when you look at the activity that took place at the time in relation to Exhibit 300, you'll see that the exhibit refers to April 17th, 1993, at 11.45 at night. And the operation is to begin on the morning of the 18th of April, at 5.30. And this is exactly what happens in Kiseljak, and the Trial Chamber found that a number of villages were ethnically cleansed. Considering the context of what took place and the number of international witnesses who described what actually took place, it's respectfully submitted that the Trial Chamber was not -- it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to determine that that left the door open for them to carry out cleansing operations. The Trial Chamber also refers to the language in Exhibit D300. This is from Colonel Blaskic to his forces referring to massacres of Croatians, "that we will be wiped out by the Mujahedin and maintain a sense of historic responsibility." I'm not sure these are the types of things that relate to combat operations, but they certainly are to instil in their forces the sense of continued fighting. Now, in light of the witnesses, including witnesses, as I recall, there was one witness specifically, BritBat, Colonel Brian Watters, who testified in relation to the HVO operations in Kiseljak. He's asked:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us stay with the 19th, Colonel. On the 19th, did the HVO continue to ethnically cleanse the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If you like, it was probably described as a mopping-up operation. I'll also ask you to recall the Vitezovi report that I just referred to, PA25. The language in there by the Vitezovi regarding their operations are "cleared". If you look at the original in B/C/S, it's the same word that's been referred to for the purposes of mopping up. So the interpretation in that case was clear, but it could have been interpreted as mopping up. And we know what happened and what the appellant conceded happened on April 16th and 18th in relation to the conduct of the Vitezovi. It's also interesting that Witness BA3 specifically indicated that he had never heard Blaskic use the word "ethnically cleanse" and that it was a word used by politicians. If you check Trial Exhibits 299 and 487, you'll see that Blaskic uses these exact words and they're interpreted from the B/C/S, and I can't pronounce the B/C/S words, but there are the two words meaning ethnically cleansing. And when he uses it, he uses it to describe what's happening to the Croatians, what's happening to the Croatian civilians. He doesn't use it to describe ever what's happening when his forces are on the ground. Why this is relevant is that Colonel Blaskic knew exactly what the words "ethnically cleanse" meant. It's in the reports. It's allegedly used by politicians. And he uses it when he incites his troops when he describes the actions of the other forces. I submit that it's obvious that he's not about to use that language in written reports to his own troops who are committing crimes as it is clear evidence of an illegal report. Now, lastly, I'd just like to refer to some of the submissions relating to the relationship between Colonel Blaskic and Dario Kordic, and you've heard the Prosecution submissions from my colleague earlier as to the relationship between the two and their responsibility. You're also fully aware that in the appeal, the appellant has indicated that he's not responsible for any crimes committed during the time that he is in Central Bosnia, June 1992 until the beginning of 1994. Despite being the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, he never had any involvement in any of the crimes committed, and we also note that the Trial Chamber found that there was not one soldier who was prosecuted for their illegal conduct in relation to the specific crimes. There is evidence that the appellants have put forward of investigations and others. That's in relation to Ahmici. And they've also indicated that there was one comment in passing to General Petkovic about the Vitezovi in relation to the truck bomb. Those are the two instances that I'm aware of. It's also interesting that Colonel Blaskic was promoted to general shortly after his time as the Central Bosnia Operative Zone [sic]. If he was a colonel which had no control over any of his forces, had no ability to prevent any of the crimes, didn't punish them, and had no ability to control units who were subordinated to him, it's just interesting that he was promoted immediately thereafter. He was the highest-ranking military commander in the operative zone, and Dario Kordic was the highest-ranking politician. Despite the comments made by some of the witnesses, when asked, Witness Watkins said - I'm sorry - when asked about the Jokers, Witness Watkins said that sources cause him to believe that the Jokers reported to Dario Kordic. And as I recall, there was one example at a checkpoint, not combat operations. BA3 testified to being taken hostage, and as the information may identify him, and you're fully aware of what his testimony is in that regard and you'll recall that in fact, and I think this was elicited from questions by Your Honour Judge Weinberg de Roca, when asked, Witness BA3 could not give an example, despite being asked twice by Your Honour of an instance where Kordic did not support him, where there was a conflict between Blaskic and subordinate troops. In the instances he gave in relation to being held hostage, in relation to checkpoints, in relation to the capturing of ammunition, he indicated in those instances where Kordic was contacted, Kordic supported him. Despite all of that, I'll just return to my opening comments that it's very telling that Blaskic never, ever indicated to anyone that it was Kordic who had control over the military police, as indicated by his presence at the checkpoints; that it was Kordic that was the one who had control over the Vitezovi, as indicated when the Vitezovi refused to release a particular individual who was held hostage. As I've indicated as well, Colonel Blaskic has not changed his position and has not presented any other evidence from himself stating the reasons why he had no idea that Colonel Kordic was in control of soldiers at a checkpoint, specifically the one he was at, where the soldiers specifically said they report to Kordic. In fact, in relation to one particular individual, an individual by the name of General Merdan, Blaskic testified at trial that there was a serious incident -- this is his testimony on February 19th, 1999. Colonel Blaskic states that: "There was another serious incident on the 15th of November, 1992, when Mr. Merdan was arrested, taken into custody, and taken to my office in the Hotel Vitez. Mr. Merdan was taken prisoner by the commander of the Vitezovi." Now, what does Colonel Blaskic indicate happens? What's his testimony about this very serious instance where he had no control over the Vitezovi? He testified: "And we succeeded, after a lot of convincing, to have him freed, and he was given back his equipment." I respectfully submit the Chamber must take with some skepticism this new-found defence, in light of the fact that Colonel Blaskic never once at trial explained that the Jokers or the Vitezovi were commanded in all respects by Kordic. In fact there's only one reference to someone else being responsible in reference to the Jokers and this is in relation to Ahmici, and it's found in a footnote of the Trial Chamber's judgement, and it indicates that the Court may -- the Trial Chamber may wish to consider that Ivica Rajic may be responsible for Ahmici. There's absolutely no evidence anywhere on the record that Ivica Rajic had anything to do with Ahmici or that he was even in the area. And if you - it's my recollection, I may be wrong - but that evidence which the Trial Chamber referred to is in closed session, and you may wish to look at that, because I can't recall, and I may be correct, I don't have it in front of me, I don't even think it was the appellant who said it was Ivica Rajic. I think it was in fact his counsel who put forward that proposition. But I stand to be corrected. When Blaskic was asked directly whether Kordic could have issued the order for Ahmici, he answered at the time of trial, years after the events in Ahmici, that he did not have any information that this was the case, and he went on to state that Kordic was not in the chain of command and he was simply a political leader. The reason he doesn't state it, the reason why he tells you in his testimony that we, and that has to be taken in light of the evidence that it's he and Dario Kordic, released the individual referred to as Mr. Merdan, is because they were working in close coordination and consultation throughout these events. As you can see from the war diary on the 16th there were 13 communications between the two of them and there's references between them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Why would Kordic and Blaskic be communicating about military matters approximately every 45 minutes on the 16th? Why is there not one written report to his superiors in Mostar indicating that he could not control the military police or the Vitezovi because they only take orders from Kordic? It's because of the two of them were working in unison. And I believe there certainly were problems. Undoubtedly there were times when the Jokers and military police appeared to want to listen to the orders of Kordic. Most of them are in relation to checkpoints and convoys, not combat operations. I'll ask that you recall Exhibit 456/109, which is a report from September 1992 which indicates that Kordic, Valenta, Blaskic, and Kostroman are the members of the working presidency of the HVO in municipalities in Central Bosnia. That's in September 1992. I'll also ask you to keep in mind Prosecution Exhibit PA3, one year later, in September 1993, an intelligence report which indicates that Blaskic is part of the Busovaca faction, that he falls under Kordic, and that who is in that faction? Kordic, Kostroman, Valenta, and includes Blaskic, the same four were the members of the working presidency one year earlier in 1992. You'll recall the testimony of Mr. Watkins, that Kordic's influence over Blaskic was significant, if not total. And that Kordic, as the senior person, would be able to instruct Blaskic, even that Kordic could give a military order to Blaskic. BA3 says Kordic had a great deal of influence over Blaskic, and in decisive moments when decisions had to be made it was Dario Kordic who made them and Blaskic who carried them out. This was a passage which was read to him and which in cross-examination he indicated that it was primarily at meetings and in relation to humanitarian matters that Kordic would instruct him and Blaskic would carry them out. First of all, if Kordic has influence over such that he can get the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone to carry out orders, regardless of whether they're humanitarian orders, that's quite telling. And secondly, it's the convoys and the keeping of -- taking of individuals and hostages at checkpoints that we find that Kordic is involved. Now, lastly, I'd just like to refer to a few transcript passages, and then I can finish, Mr. President, or as it's been an hour and a half, I can take a break now, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We'll break in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You'll recall that the Defence has referred to this press conference on April 27th, where Blaskic indicated he was horrified as to what happened in Ahmici. Keep in mind that about ten days later, on May 5th, on a meeting between Kordic and representatives of the Special Rapporteur for the UN Commission on Human Rights, when asked about Ahmici, Dario Kordic, on May 5th, says: "The atrocities were either committed by Serbs who had infiltrated in the night or the Muslims themselves committed the atrocities against their own people to get international sympathy." Four days later, on May 9th, this is once again after the press conference both Blaskic and Kordic were at, at a meeting between the commander of the British Battalion and Colonel Blaskic, Blaskic gave his view as to how the massacre in Ahmici occurred. General Duncan testified that Blaskic stated that it was Serb extremists who came into Ahmici, or Muslims who had infiltrated the pocket were dressed in HVO uniforms. This is exactly what Kordic said four days earlier. The individual who he has no relationship with and who is just a political authority. Brigadier Duncan, quite correctly in my submission, found his reasons for the events in Ahmici to be ridiculous. Witness BA3 stated he would be flabbergasted by such an as such an assertion as to what happened in Ahmici. And the language used in that meeting to General Duncan by Blaskic are echoed in the Danas article six months later, in October 1993. The article that Blaskic says was written essentially by someone else. If that's the case it's certainly a coincidence that similar language and similar explanations as to who committed the crimes in Ahmici are found in a news article which echo the comments made by Colonel Blaskic himself to the commander of BritBat. And lastly, there has been submissions and evidence about Blaskic being a professional soldier. There was ample evidence of this at trial as well. This isn't new. I'd just like to read to you in closing in my submissions what Colonel Stewart, the commander of the British battalion, said in relation to Colonel Blaskic. I'm now quoting from the transcript of the testimony of Colonel Stewart: "I would like to end by giving my impression and opinion. I want to place on record that personally I have a great liking for Tihomir Blaskic. That was until the massacre of Ahmici. I considered him someone I could trust and who was good for his word and a professional officer, and I was disappointed in his response after the massacre in Ahmici. I know that Mr. Blaskic was ex-Yugoslav National Army, and so was Mr. Merdan. They knew one another well. To start with, I always considered Tihomir Blaskic was the commander. Kordic was a complication. But I knew from my sources that the HVO didn't think of him as a soldier in the same way as they thought of Tihomir Blaskic. After all, Kordic always told me he was the vice-president of the HVO and his background as I understand it was that of a journalist." Then he continues: "As I have mentioned at times we, the British, were confused as to the command structure, particularly complicated by Kordic, but Blaskic was the main link to Petkovic, a chief of staff of HVO and I saw them a couple of times together, not Kordic. I am positive that the HVO carried out the massacres, the major massacres in the Lasva Valley in April 1993. I find it very difficult to believe that the HVO command in Vitez did not know or did not order the attack on the village of Ahmici, which is only 3.5 kilometres from the Hotel Vitez. I do not believe that any command structure doesn't know what's happening with the soldiers that short a distance away. And in conclusion, despite my great personal liking for Tihomir Blaskic, I believe that Tihomir Blaskic alone was the HVO commander in Central Bosnia and thus held command responsibility for the actions of his soldiers." Those are the submissions on this matter. I'm sorry for taking five minutes over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Farrell. We break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On today's transcript page 35, line 12, you referred us to a footnote in the Trial Chamber judgement without quoting this footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could, after the break, just give us the footnote, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we break now and we resume at 10.45. The Prosecution will have 20 more minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please be seated. So we resume the hearing, and I'll give the floor to the Prosecution for 20 minutes. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Ms. Michelle Jarvis will be making the remaining Prosecution submissions, and I will ask her to do so in just one minute. I just wanted to note one thing. I realised after the submissions, first of all, in answer to a question of Your Honour Judge Schomburg, in the Trial Chamber's judgement footnote 904, at page 144 is the reference I think that may assist Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The second matter, if I could just clarify: I referred to Colonel Blaskic's testimony during the trial in relation to an incident where an individual by the name of Mr. Merdan was taken to Colonel Blaskic's -- was arrested, taken into custody, and taken to his office. Just looking at his testimony at the break, I just thought I should make it clear that it says that Merdan was arrested, taken into custody, and taken to Blaskic's office in the Hotel Vitez, where another individual was present, General Prkacin was there, together with Blaskic. He had been taken prisoner by the commander of the Vitezovi. And the date is November 15th, 1992. That's the date in the testimony of Colonel Blaskic on February 19th, 1999. I note that there are some documents before you regarding the incident on November 1992. They're Exhibits 87 to the Defence first motion, and Exhibit 33 to the Defence fourth motion. I just want to bring those to your attention because they appear to November 15th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that. I didn't want to leave the impression that they're the exact same incident because I'm not sure on the basis of the evidence. I will now ask my colleague Ms. Jarvis to make the remaining submissions for the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will be making the Prosecution's submissions in relation to the appellant's ground of appeal concerning Article 5 of the Statute and a few related evidentiary issues that come up in the context of that ground of appeal. The only thing that the appellant has so far said about his Article 5 ground of appeal is that he does not believe the Trial Chamber's analysis of discriminatory intent for persecution was properly done. The Prosecution can only assume that to support this argument, he relies on the positions set out in his appeal brief, and there are certainly a number of things that the Prosecution wishes to address in relation to those submissions. In particular, Your Honours, the appellant seeks to advance the most restrictive possible legal definition of persecution. As I'll explain, the elements that he proposes are contrary to the Tribunal's established jurisprudence. But even if the legal propositions he suggests were correct, the facts of this case would indeed meet those requirements. In a nutshell, the appellant's position is one of denial. He denies that the objective of the Bosnian Croat leadership in Central Bosnia was to remove the Muslim population from the targeted areas. Quite simply, he denies that there was any ethnic cleansing in Central Bosnia at all. The evidence overwhelmingly contradicts this, Your Honours. Reflecting back on the voluminous evidentiary record in this case, the Trial Chamber, at paragraph 750, looked at the systematic plundering and burning to the ground of houses and stables, the targeting of civilians, regardless of age or gender; the destruction of religious institutions, the mosques; the systematic campaign of detentions, which was organised, prisoners being transferred from one detention centre to another, prisoners being systematically taken after every military attack. The accused himself stated that 20 or so villages were attacked, according to a pattern which never - excuse me - changed. The Trial Chamber concluded that the only reasonable inference was that the objective was to make the Muslim population take flight. The comments of a Canadian army officer, reflecting back over the aftermath of the attacks in Kiseljak, are reflective of the evidence about the overall campaign. He said: "The impression it left with me is very vivid and very striking, because I was taken aback by the surgical nature of the damage. As you drove through this area, there would be houses that were burnt out. There would be one or two or three, and then right in the middle of them, you'd see another house that was completely intact, inhabited even. And then further down the road, more destroyed houses." He continued: "Upon talking to the inhabitants, it quickly became apparent that the damaged houses belonged to Bosnian Muslims and the undamaged ones were the property of Bosnian Croats." He concluded: "I think it was very discriminating." In light of evidence such as this, Your Honours, the appellants claim that there was no ethnic cleansing is unsustainable. The appellant even goes so far in his brief as to deny that the crimes of which he was convicted are sufficiently grave to constitute persecution. Let's not forget that what is at issue here is systematic targeting of Bosnian Muslim civilians, with murder and serious bodily injury; systematic detention, in cruel and inhumane circumstances; forcible transfer; and the destruction of their homes and livelihood, in more than 20 villages, across three municipalities, throughout the course of an entire year. The appellant further denies that he acted in furtherance of the ethnic cleansing campaign. He maintains his position primarily by pointing out that he was not known to use discriminatory language in relation to Muslims. Obviously, though, Your Honours, his discriminatory actions speak far louder than his words. Your Honours, having given this general overview, I'll turn to the specific legal and evidentiary propositions that the appellant's raised in relation to Article 5. My submissions will be divided into four main areas. The first one is the appellant's claim that the mens rea standard adopted by the Trial Chamber was erroneous. Secondly, I'll look specifically at the evidence regarding General Blaskic's discriminatory intent in this case. Third, I will look at the Trial Chamber's findings regarding the three specific villages mentioned yesterday by the appellant, Donja Veceriska, Gacice, and Grbavica. And fourth, I'd like to touch briefly on the appellant's arguments regarding the civilian nature of the population in Stari Vitez, because that is, of course, an important contextual element for crimes against humanity. Your Honours, turning, then, to the first topic, the correct mens rea standard for persecution. The appellant's arguments regarding the mens rea standard for persecution and the Trial Chamber's alleged error start from the erroneous position that for persecution, proof of a state or organisational policy to exclude the victims from society or humanity is required. Well, Your Honours, the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber in the Krnojelac case makes it clear that no such policy element is required, and I direct you to the definition of persecution set out at paragraph 185. In fact, in overturning the acquittals of Mr. Krnojelac on the crime of persecution and entering convictions, the Appeals Chamber made absolutely no reference to any requirement that there be a policy to remove victims from society or humanity. In our submission, the jurisprudence on that point is settled. As an aside, though, Your Honours, even if the appellant was correct that this was a requirement, the facts of this case, indeed the Trial Chamber found that such a policy did exist. The Trial Chamber in the judgement documents a policy stemming from President Tudjman in Croatia, down through the authorities in Central Bosnia, to annex the so-called Croatian territories of Bosnia to Croatia. When the Vance-Owen Peace Plan failed to deliver the territories coveted, the Bosnian Croats issued an ultimatum to the ABiH, an ultimatum which was rejected. This was the stage upon which the Bosnian Croat political and military leadership unleashed their coordinated campaign of military attacks. They could not be a clearer example of a policy to remove the targeted group from society or humanity. Your Honours, having erroneously claimed that persecution requires this policy element, the appellant then asserts that the Trial Chamber erred by failing to require that General Blaskic subscribe to that policy. That's what he suggests the mens rea for persecution requires. Again, this argument is easily disposed of. There is no such policy requirement for persecution, and the Trial Chamber's failure to require it certainly demonstrates no error. Although the appellant criticises the Trial Chamber for equating the mens rea requirement for persecution with proof of specific intent to target because the victim belongs to a particular community or group, in fact, that accords exactly with the definition set down by the Appeals Chamber in the Krnojelac case, and I direct you to paragraphs 184 and 185 in that regard. This also accords overwhelmingly with the Trial Chamber's jurisprudence on the mens rea of persecution. In Kupreskic, the Trial Chamber referred to attacking persons on account of their political or religious affiliations. In Kvocka, to the fact that the detainees in Omarska camp were selected on the basis of their affiliation with the group. The Prosecution also notes that this formulation is consistent with Article 7 of the ICC Statute, which also refers to targeting by reason of the identity of the group. Your Honours, turning then to my next topic, the evidence of General Blaskic's discriminatory intent in this case. Notwithstanding the arguments that the appellant made yesterday, the Prosecution's rebuttal evidence amply demonstrates that the appellant barely raised an eyebrow in response to the devastating crimes committed against the population in Central Bosnia. In Exhibit PA38, dated the 22nd of June, 1993, General Blaskic sang the praises of the Vitezovi, pleaded that they not be disbanded, and justified their behaviour on the basis that they simply kicked over the traces a little. This stands in stark contrast to the evidence of Witness BA2, who recounted how General Blaskic hauled him over the coals in response to a simple breach in military dress code. He was threatened with imprisonment. The disparity in General Blaskic's reaction speaks volumes about the discriminatory underpinnings of his conduct. The appellant has relied on the fact that witnesses said he was not known to use derogatory language about Muslims. In fact, as my colleague Mr. Farrell mentioned, there was considerable evidence to this same effect at trial, and it's conveniently recounted in the appellant's brief at pages 177 to 178. Notwithstanding all of this evidence, the Trial Chamber nevertheless determined that the appellant was acting with discriminatory intent. How can this be reconciled? Because the evidence clearly discloses that General Blaskic was skilled at tailoring his remarks depending on the nature of his audience. For example, the duplicity in General Blaskic's response to Ahmici was specifically noted by the Trial Chamber at paragraph 483. His comments to Colonel Stewart, on the one hand, expressing utmost concern about the crimes, and yet that very same day, in a report up the chain of command, expressing no remorse or anger about what happened, and in fact complaining that the international community presented a biased account of these events. And Mr. Farrell has explained that General Duncan's testimony at trial accords precisely with the account recorded in the Danas article about General Blaskic's denial of the crimes in Ahmici and the completely unacceptable explanations that he sought to advance about the causes of that attack. Indeed, many witnesses on appeal expressed surprise, and in some cases even outrage, at some of the conduct that has indisputably been attributed to General Blaskic. Witness BA1, while maintaining that the appellant always conducted himself professionally, categorically stated that the use of prisoners for trench-digging was illegal. Yet we know, from Exhibit PA56, that General Blaskic expressed concern to the Kiseljak Brigade about the international community finding out about trench-digging, but expressed no concern about the practice itself. Your Honours, there is also one very important matter that I would like to draw to your attention, and it builds on Mr. Farrell's comments yesterday and today about the appellant's erroneous claim at trial that the ABiH initiated the attacks on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Jarvis. I'm told you're probably speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll endeavour to slow down, and my apologies to the interpreters. Why would he simply not have said the HVO attacked, the HVO was on the offensive? The inference that must be drawn from this false defence is that the appellant knew full well the illegal and discriminatory objective underlying the attacks that he was directing, and he was attempting to provide a shield to cover his actions to the world at large. Your Honours, just very quickly, because I am running out of time, I wanted to address the Trial Chamber's findings regarding Donja Veceriska, Gacice, and Grbavica, because the appellant suggested yesterday that the Trial Chamber applied an incorrect standard in relation to those three villages, and you'll recall Your Honour Judge Schomburg pointed out the discrepancy in the translation between the original French and the English, "dolus eventualis" in the French version, "negligence" in the English. It's clear as Ms. Boelaert pointed out in her submissions yesterday, that the Trial Chamber applied a dolus eventualis standard which is in accordance with the Tribunal's jurisprudence on indirect intent, as confirmed most recently in the Galic judgement. One thing that I wanted to say, because it's relevant to the issue of persecution, is that in finding indirect intent regarding these three villages, the Trial Chamber was looking at the general intent requirement for the actus reus of the crimes. It's not an indirect intent finding regarding the specific discriminatory intent for persecution. He may have indirectly intended the commission of the crimes, but General Blaskic took the risk of those crimes being committed because the victims of the crimes would be Muslims. He sent troops in knowing full well that they were very likely to commit crimes against Muslims and it's part of the same discriminatory process underpinning the rest of his actions. Alternatively, Your Honours, if you are of the view that these villages could not be sustained under Article 7(1), certainly they could be sustained as persecution under Article 7(3), and the Krnojelac appeals judgement confirms that Article 7(3) does indeed apply to specific intent crimes such as persecution. Very quickly, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Ms. Jarvis, I'm sorry, but your time has expired.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS

utterances.text: I'd just like to direct Your Honours' attention to the Prosecution's closing brief at trial regarding Stari Vitez. Your Honours, in conclusion, I'd just like to return to the theme that I started with, and that is the appellant's denial about what happened in this case. Your Honours, he was a commander in a position of special responsibility as a guardian of international law. Thank you very much for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR

JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have mixed feelings in that regard, Your Honour. On the one hand, I'd like more time. On the other hand, I'm looking forward to finishing this case after seven years. Tribunal Prosecutor, because none of them here that have presented to Your Honours tried the case. They didn't see the evidence come in. utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you find that an incredible explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I just remember laughing myself sick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that Colonel Blaskic never made such an explanation to you for Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would definitely agree that Colonel Blaskic never made such a statement to me, that the Serbs were responsible for that action, which, of course, goes to show, you know, that Kordic was not a soldier; otherwise, he would not have made such an outrageous statement. Stewart was there. Duncan made a mistake. We heard about this mistake over and over and over again at trial. And now the appellate Prosecutors are repeating this mistake in an attempt, as innocently as it may be, to prejudice you and inflame you against the appellant, so that you'll believe that he lied, he covered up, he pointed at the Serbs, and it's not true. He never said it. Now, there was another mistake made yesterday, and it involves the statement by one of my learned colleagues with respect to Defence Exhibit 410. She said 410 is identical to Exhibit 1 to the first Rule 115 motion and that our statements to you, our written and oral submissions that the Ahmici report from the 26th - excuse me - that the Ahmici report from the 26th of November, 1993, that that wouldn't have changed the trial at all, because the same report was already in evidence at trial. And the exhibit cited was D410. Well, first, let's look very quickly at Exhibit 1 to the first Rule 115 motion so we have it in mind. Here's the cover page.
