utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just so there's some logic and order to my comments, I will first go back and try and cover legal issues, some of the legal issues that were raised yesterday, and then follow with a reply to some of the issues raised this morning. Counsel stated yesterday, at page 130 in the transcript, that "it is beyond comprehension how a general who orders attacks of a village could justifiably hope that serious violations of international law, such as murders and cruel and inhumane treatment, would not occur." That was said. And the implication, Your Honours, is that any fighting in built-up areas is per se illegal under international law. As was customary, unfortunately, in the civil war in Bosnia, military units were housed in villages. If one military force deemed it necessary to take a military action against a military unit housed in a village, that required a military action directed at that unit in the village, and that's absolutely legal under the law that you are bound to enforce so long as there's a military objective and there are no disproportionate civilian casualties. That seems to be entirely lost on the Prosecutor's office. We might want to live in a world where war is illegal, but we don't, and this is not a legislative body. Now, with respect to 7(1) and 7(3) liability, counsel across the well argued that if it finds appellant's conviction under 7(1) to be defective, you can revise the conviction and find him guilty under 7(3). And she said that this would not be a notice problem for appellant. We respectfully submit this misses the point. It appears from the judgement appellant has already been convicted below under both 7(1) and 7(3). The prejudice is: We were forced to try this case and respond to two inconsistent theories simultaneously, and that's a definition, the definition, the most basic definition, of a defective indictment. We also don't have a valid judgement document, because the judgement does not articulate a clear theory of liability. It conflates 7(1) and 7(3). There was no trial where appellant had fair and full notice of the charges. What we had was an ex post facto selection of a theory of criminal liability based on a menu available to the Trial Chamber. But the most fundamental problem is: We never knew specifically what theory we were defending against and which might take precedence, which is just underscored by the comments of the Prosecutor that if you find one is bad, well, switch over to the other. As we read the Kupreskic appeals judgement, the remedy is reversal in toto for that fact. Now, there was also the argument made that effective control of the forces in question are irrelevant. That question is irrelevant to the case because appellant was convicted of issuing orders under 7(1), and that you don't have to look at effective control. We have spent a lot of time the last three years in this appeal writing briefs and submitting materials to you on effective control, I submit, and it's a little odd for the Prosecutor now to be claiming effective control is irrelevant. In fact, her argument was entirely circular. Appellant was principally convicted of issuing orders under 7(1), on the basis of his alleged superior relationship and control over subordinate units, i.e., because he controlled the units and because they committed crimes, ergo he must have ordered them. So you see, to assume away the relevance of effective control and say he ordered, he issued orders, that's all we have to know, that is a circular argument where the conclusion that orders were given is based on the assumption that effective control existed. That's what she asked you to do yesterday. Now, what about the orders themselves? I've talked about the circular argument made yesterday by counsel. But there are three instances, I believe, in the judgement where the Trial Chamber looked at specific orders and said: This is an illegal order. D269, D299, and D300. Now, we heard a little bit from Mr. Farrell this morning trying to resurrect an argument that these orders were illegal. I want to note that at trial, in the trial in this case lasted 26 months, they were afraid to ask a single witness whether these orders were illegal. They never brought in a military expert or any other military qualified person and said: Hey, is this an illegal order? They never did it. They made a decision at trial not to do it because they knew they couldn't sustain it. But now that the Trial Chamber jumped in the water and got all wet, they're trying to defend it. There's no basis in the record for it. Indeed, the record is what you heard last week from multiple witnesses. Every witness, every witness to opine on these orders in this case said they're legal, and with respect to D269, it's a defensive order. That's the only testimony you have. So if you've somehow find that the Trial Chamber had a rational basis for its finding you're going to have to go outside the evidence because it's not in the evidence, it's not in the testimony. It's just not there. That is with respect to D269, D267, and PA12. What about D299 and D300? Those are the Kiseljak orders that were discussed yesterday by Mr. Nobilo. He focussed on those orders and he also made, I think, an interesting discovery with respect to a section of the war diary that had been blurred with a prior entry, and now hopefully we have that clarified. He made very clear, if you take those three documents together and you take the map, you have a picture of a commander who is repeatedly, in blunt and direct language, instructing Mario Bradara, the deputy commander of the Kiseljak Brigade: Go up the hill and take the high ground. Stay out of the village. Don't go down below. It's absolutely clear from the orders and the war diary that is what he was trying to do. And he repeated it. He said it multiple times. And yet, he was convicted of actions that units of that brigade took, going exactly where he told them not to go, because they went into the villages and they got into trouble and they committed crimes. There's one other point I'd like to make about these exhibits. 267, 268, 269, 299, 300. They all start with a D. That means they were not presented in the Prosecutor's case in chief. They didn't have them. They would have been produced to us as statements of the accused pre-trial if they had had them. They didn't have them. They didn't get them in their investigation, they didn't present them to the judge that returned the indictment against our client. They didn't present them in their case in chief. They were produced in the Defence case, for the first time, and one can ask, and I submit should ask: Was it responsible? Was it reckless, for Richard Goldstone to bring this indictment against the accused when he lacked the basic documents, documenting the events in question? He didn't have them. And that's how this case was tried. This case was tried with a year of victim testimony, with almost no mention of the accused. We sat there and listened to a year of victim testimony, a horrible experience, one of the worst experiences in my life, listening to victims with their very tragic stories. Now, although it's distasteful, I need to address the Rule 68 issue. The Prosecution has confirmed that it engaged in Rule 68 violations vis-a-vis the Kordic case evidence and specific witnesses. There's no explanation for these violations in the record. With respect to Witness BA1, the Prosecutor admitted yesterday that non-production of his statement was a violation of Rule 68, but he argues: We got the reporter's transcript at the end of 1999, some four months after trial was concluded, so there's no prejudice. What is important is the statement was given in August of 1996. The Trial Chamber issued an order pursuant to our Rule 68 motion that exculpatory material had to be identified, and either produced or a statement submitted to the Court why it couldn't be produced. Not only was Rule 68 violated; that order was violated. The Trial Chamber below was misled. We did get the transcript of this particular witness at the end of 1999 from the Registrar's Office, together with boxes of other transcripts, voluminous materials, and it took us some time to get through them. When we got through them, we brought them to the Court's attention. Now, my learned colleague, and again he inherited this problem to a very, very large extent and I'm not in any way suggesting that he was involved in the events in 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999, but he did suggest that the sanction, the proper sanction for this violation is to sanction the Prosecutor's office, like imposing a fine on them payable to the library fund or something like that. With all due respect, where a party is damaged and prejudiced, the remedy must address the damage. How can you address the damage? And I have -- I'm not done talking about the violations, but I'll continue talking about the remedy. How can you -- how can the Prosecutor argue with a straight face that there's been no prejudice when they do not agree that the evidence should be reviewed de novo? They want you to give great deference to the Trial Chamber's findings, which, if you do that, it basically guts the new evidence. You either look at the evidence de novo, apply a "proof beyond a reasonable doubt" standard, which is what you could do to avoid prejudice from the Rule 68 violation, or else the prejudice to appellant is horrific. It's horrific. And in the American and in the British systems, an acquittal or new trial would be required, given the volume of Rule 68 violations here. What were the others? Mr. Watkins gave a statement on the 1st of June, 1996. It was not produced. It was not disclosed. That statement contains extensive exculpatory information. The Prosecutor suggests: Well, it really wasn't prejudicial because the appellant already knew about the Convoy of Joy. It is true appellant was consulted in connection with that event. He was not omnipotently on the scene. That convoy was some 500 vehicles long. To suggest that he had complete information about that incident is simply not credible. And in any event, evidence from the witness is different from evidence from a neutral international -- neutral observer. That's all I should say concerning BA -- well, Mr. Watkins, I'm sorry, he was a public witness. A military expert, a neutral independent expert. There's a huge difference in the quantum of evidence for Mr. Watkins to say: This is what I saw. This is what I heard. Based on this event and everything else, the Jokers were controlled by Kordic. And this is the view that ECMM had. It wasn't just me. That's what Watkins said. To suggest that somehow that testimony was within the power of the appellant to give himself on the stand is preposterous and also ignores that the Watkins statement contains numerous other important pieces of information concerning command and control problems within the HVO, existence of isolated pockets and the impact on C2 from that fact.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. After all these years, it's still an exciting case. It also fails to note, very critically, that -- Well, let me preface this with counsel also said: Witness Duncan testified about the Convoy of Joy so we don't need Watkins's statement. There's no prejudice. What did Duncan say? If you look at his testimony, reporter's transcript 9028 to 9227, Duncan said there was a problem with the police. Kordic was there, Kordic helped sort it out. Duncan never identifies the military police as the problem with the Convoy of Joy, never identifies the Jokers. The key information in the Watkins statement that Kordic controlled the Jokers is not in Duncan's testimony. We didn't get it. We didn't have the opportunity to present it to the Trial Chamber. That's a serious problem. And I am sorry Your Honours have inherited it, but it's now your problem. The Prosecutor contend that had it produced BA3's statement to us many years ago. They did not claim that when they opposed our second Rule 115 motion. There is a much larger body of withheld exculpatory evidence, and it is in the record in this case. If you look at our second Rule 115 motion, there are seven witnesses in addition to the ones I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They are Witness AO, Witness Dragutin Cicak, Witness I, Witness T, Ekrem Mahmutovic, Zdenko Rajic, Witness Z. All provided exculpatory information in Kordic, not provided to us in a timely manner. Indeed, there are additional documents from the Kordic case that we were not provided in addition to those, many of those that you've received, such as Exhibit 16 to the second Rule 115 motion, Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: -- Exhibit 2022, and Exhibits 23 and 24. So you must look, we submit, not only at the Rule 16 violation, but the violations of the Trial Chamber's order issued in 1996 concerning the production of specific categories of exculpatory information and evidence to the appellant. You'll recall from yesterday our motion was very specific. Our potential theory of the Defence was very clear to all. Everyone was on notice where we wanted to go in defending our client. Now, Mr. Farrell suggested that he may want to supplement the record on these questions. Well, they've already responded in the form of the Rule 115 motions to the availability and unavailability, et cetera, issue. So they've already had their opportunity, we submit, to speak to those issues. And any attempt, any further attempt to supplement the record, it is appellant's position, must be accompanied by an evidentiary hearing at which the investigators and the Prosecutors, in both the Kordic and Blaskic cases, are produced, with all of their records, all the witness statements, all their investigative notes, in advance of the hearing. And if we want to dig deeper into it, that's the way to do it, not to have Mr. Farrell stand up and represent or submit a declaration that he's conducted some discussions with people in his office and concluded A, B, or C, with all due respect. And I finally point out: Whether or not a document or a witness was accepted pursuant to our Rule 115 motions is not the standard as to whether it was exculpatory and should have been produced under Rule 68. There are two different standards. So there are witnesses and exhibits that you chose not to admit from the Rule 115 evidence that still would meet the exculpatory standard of Rule 68, which I make that point for two reasons: One, so when you're looking at the scope of the evidence that was wrongfully is you pressed you can define the scope; and two, in terms of the prejudice, that material hasn't even been added to the record. We'll never have a chance to present that evidence on behalf of our client. That is lasting, permanent prejudice. I'd like now to turn to a subject that is going to shame my grammar school French, dolus eventualis. Is it Latin? There you go. That's true shame. I guess we're talking about the French version of the judgement, which misled me. Although I query if a Latin phrase was used, why wouldn't that have been repeated in the English judgement? That's a bit of a mystery to me. But in any event, we are where we are, and I want to address the question. Our position, and it is set forth in more detail in our appellant brief, is that the Trial Chamber actually applied a standard much lower than dolus eventualis, even though it may have cited to a dolus eventualis standard. For example, in paragraph 562 of the judgement, it notes that 7(1) liability is being imposed because the appellant "ordered acts which he could only reasonably have anticipated would lead to crimes." That is a reasonably foreseeable standard. A reasonably foreseeable standard is a negligence standard, whereas dolus eventualis is a standard we believe in all systems which is closer to recklessness, indeed wilful blindness is the term that would most closely define it, I believe, in my legal system, in my national legal system. That is, a person who chooses not to acquire knowledge that would have put them directly on notice of the risk of harm. So that is our principal concern with respect to the use, with respect to the Gacice and Donja Veceriska items of this standard. We don't believe an appropriate standard was used, as defined by the Trial Chamber. So even if the term is used, and the term may well be an appropriate standard, as defined by the Trial Chamber, it was misdefined, misconstrued and applied in an impermissible way. It's also not clear from the judgement whether dolus eventualis was used in some way in connection with 7(3) liability. And we submit that it could not have been the case, and because there's ambiguity, that is a further error in the judgement. 7(3) imposes liability for a failure to take action, not for a failure to acquire knowledge of a commander's subordinates' acts. And there's a quote here from the Celebici Appeals Chamber judgement at paragraph 226 that is on point, and I quote: "The point here should be that knowledge may not be presumed if (the accused) had the means to obtain the knowledge but deliberately refrained from doing so. The argument that a breach of the duty of a superior to remain constantly informed of his subordinates' actions will necessarily result in criminal liability, comes close to the imposition of criminal liability on a strict or negligence basis." We submit that, with respect to Gacice and Donja Veceriska, as well as generally, the evidence did not satisfy either standard, either a higher dolus eventualis standard or even the lower standard articulated by the Trial Chamber. I think one of the examples in that paragraph of the judgement is that because in October of 1992 there was an incident and houses were burned in Novi Travnik, and Colonel Blaskic issued an order directing that all units, Novi Travnik units, et cetera, be informed that conduct is inappropriate, it must stop, et cetera, et cetera, that that was notice that come April, in Vitez, Colonel Blaskic had this mental state such that any use of any military unit exposed him to strict liability for their later conduct. That simply cannot be the case. That cannot be the standard in international law, or else we have come within a hair of saying: War is illegal. You can look at operations in Iraq. There are mistakes made. There are civilians killed. There is a possibility that that's going to happen any time you send a patrol with a military mission, particularly into a built-up area, looking for a suspect, for example, or any time you drop a bomb, there can be civilian casualties. Does that mean you can never do any of those things and it's illegal to do it if the activity ever results in a civilian death? Of course not. The discussion concerning artillery and infantry became somewhat transformed yesterday, and I'd like to comment on that. We had been talking about the use in the judgement of the artillery, followed by infantry pattern as a type of signature pattern from which the Trial Chamber drew certain inferences, but yesterday the Prosecutor said: No, that's not why we are interested in artillery. We are interested in artillery because it shows that Blaskic ordered all these attacks because he alone controlled the artillery. Again, that -- I'm sure that's a belief that counsel holds in good faith, but counsel has a lack of understanding of the evidence in the case, and I need to point you to the details. Appellant testified that he commanded the large artillery, such as the Nora Howitzer, that's N-o-r-a, that was the name of the gun, which was a 152-millimetre artillery device, but that other weapons, such as mortars, were not within his control. Those were infantry weapons. Every platoon, whatever, had its own mortar or RPG. And that was borne out in the testimony with respect to, for example, Ahmici. Was artillery used in Ahmici? You see it in a lot of the documents. People talk about artillery, shells coming in. Question by Judge Rodrigues at transcript page 23880: "Was artillery used in Ahmici?" Answer by Colonel Stewart: "I don't think so. I think it was mortars, but I'm not certain." Even the Prosecutor's own investigator, Mr. Akhavan, testified at transcript page 5367: "There were a number of factors which led us to believe it was an organised operation." He's referring to Ahmici. "For one thing, the use of mortars, rocket-propelled grenades and other such semi-heavy weaponry suggested it could not have been, let us say, a band of just a few people carrying guns, ordinary guns." 52-millimetre mortars, 62 millimetre mortars, RPGs, rocket-propelled grenades, those are all infantry weapons. There's no evidence - and other witness were asked, no evidence - that walls in Ahmici were blown through by heavy shells. The houses were burned in Ahmici. There was a crime, make no mistake about it. No evidence of heavy artillery. It's not there. The Prosecutor's point is irrelevant. And indeed, the Prosecutor herself admitted in closing argument at the trial that that was the case, that there were these other weapons, mortars, et cetera, that were infantry weapons. See closing argument of the Prosecutor 27 July 1999 at transcript page 143. Now I want to touch for a moment on legal authority to discipline. I want to refer you to page 88 of our brief, with respect to substantial discussion of the fact that while appellant had the authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings over regular HVO soldiers for infractions of military discipline, that is a different thing from any criminal matter. Criminal matters, under the laws in place in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, had to be referred to the military district courts and the military prosecutors. Appellant had no authority to initiate a criminal prosecution, and that's why you see him writing to the military police, writing to SIS, saying: Conduct an investigation, and I want you to forward your report to the military prosecutor, district military prosecutor's office. They were the authority that had the lawful authority to institute criminal prosecutions. So when you hear about Colonel Blaskic telling a foot soldier: "Get rid of those tennis shoes or I'm going to take care of you," we're talking about discipline. We're talking about military discipline, not shaving, not having a clean uniform, that kind of thing, which is not particularly relevant to this case. The issues in this case involve criminal conduct. Now, there was a citation yesterday to Slavko Marin, for the proposition that appellant actually had authority to punish the military police and the Vitezovi, which is not correct. And Marin actually testified, at the page cited, which is reporter's transcript 13970, that: "For a member of the Vitezovi, a disciplinary measure can be imposed only by the commander of the Vitezovi, and not General Blaskic. For a member of the military police, it is only a commander of the military police that can carry out this disciplinary action."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My apologies. A word about Witness PT. There was a comment yesterday that Witness PT established that in fact the HVO knew and received reports that there had been a crime in Ahmici as of April 18th, 1993. If you look -- he -- Witness PT used that date, and this is another example of a clear error that keeps being repeated and repeated and repeated. But if you look at the testimony, Witness PT said he learned about Ahmici -- I think we better go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now I will turn to the comments this morning by my learned counsel across the well. You have heard repeatedly that there was an attack on 20 villages simultaneously on April 16th. For some perspective on this claim, I suggest, if you look at a map, you'll see first of all four of those so-called villages are actually Ahmici. Ahmici is comprised and is adjacent to Ahmici, Santici, Nadioci, and Pirici. They're all hamlets, they're all very small, they're all adjacent to one another. They were all attacked in this activity by the Jokers and the military police. So that's four right there. It's really one location, but that's four by the Prosecutor's counting. Then you have Gacice and Donja Veceriska, in the Vitez municipality, and I note in passing that, while the Prosecutor's central thesis is: Everything that happened was organised and simultaneous on the 20th of April, if you look at the evidence in the case, I think it's the case of Gacice, there was actually negotiation for three or four days, between the HVO unit and the Territorial Defence unit, over what would happen. Nothing happened for three or four days while they negotiated. Hardly an indication that someone issued an order: Go attack 20 villages tomorrow morning at 5.30. If that order was issued, it sure wasn't followed in Gacice. And then you have two villages in the Busovaca area for which appellant was convicted, two tiny hamlets, Loncari and Ocehnici. One on the 17th and one on the 19th. They're not on the 16th. Where's the master plan? Where's the simultaneous attack at 5.30 a.m. on the 16th. One of those is a village of 5 or 6 homes, 33 inhabitants. Everything else, Your Honours, is in Kiseljak. And wasn't attacked on the 16th of April. There were no attacks in Kiseljak on the 16th of April. So this idea that there's a simultaneous attack on 20 villages at 5.30 a.m. on the 16th of April is a fiction, a very convenient fiction, but a fiction nonetheless. And the evidence in the trial record is absolutely clear on each of the villages that I identified. May I inquire what our schedule is so I can just organise my work as efficiently as possible, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, we will continue for 15 minutes now, and then break for 20, 25 minutes, and then resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very good. That's helpful. Thank you. Could we call up PA12, please. This morning Mr. Farrell went back to PA12, which is the order to the military police at 0130 on the 16th of April. And again took the position that they never pursued at trial, never questioned a witness, never got any witness at trial to say this was a combat order, yet Mr. Farrell argued to you this morning: By golly, counsel says this is a combat order. If you look at that order and you'll need to push your "computer evidence" button to see it -- it does use the word "combat order" in the instruction. But you've got to read the whole phrase: "Combat order on securing the section of the road and repelling any attack." And if you read paragraph 2, it's absolutely clear. It's an order to block. It's an order to block approaches to the road. And in case of an attack, by precision fire repel the enemy. Precision means carefully targeted, the opposite of burning houses and killing civilians. Now, then Mr. Farrell suggested that there had been some kind of a trick in the appellant's testimony at trial, and at 8.59 this morning - I don't know if there's another way to identify the transcript - he pulled up a question, or he read a question to appellant in his testimony to the effect of: Other than the order 267, were there any other orders to the military police on the 15th of April? Answer: No. I'm no sure that counsel intended to suggest that this exhibit, PA12, was inconsistent with that answer, but this exhibit of course is an order from the 16th of April. It's not an order from the 15th. Now I'd like to just briefly step through the meetings and the orders on the 15th to 16th of April, because counsel did address that, and I think it was done, unfortunately, in a bit of a fuzzy way, about midway through this I'll need to go into short private session. The sequence of events begins on the 15th with D267, a preparatory order to repel terrorist activity. Your Honours will remember that very morning an HVO brigade commander, Zivko Totic, the Zenica Brigade commander, was kidnapped, his entourage of four were shot dead. The pictures are in the record. You can look at a videotape looking at a car full of bullet holes, et cetera, et cetera, a pretty ugly scene. And that order, 267, is specifically directed to preparing to repel and be on the alert for other terrorist activities, because it is well known that a general attack can be preceded by attempts to liquidate the command structure, command structure or brigade commanders and higher commanders. If you can liquidate your opponents' command structure, there are no commanders left for when you launch a more general attack. So 267 goes out. Then, and now we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Farrell discussed four exhibits this morning, which are PA6, 7, 8, and 10, all for the proposition that the Vitez Brigade was in Ahmici on the 16th of April. I note -- if you took those reports and you listed all the different villages and locations that are discussed in those reports, you'd have a list of -- I don't know if it's 8 or 12, a lot of different locations, all within the Vitez municipality, not within the orders and directions given to the Vitez Brigade, and in the case of, for example Ahmici, exclusively in the province of the orders given to the military police to go to the road below Ahmici and secure it. So with all due respect to my colleague, these are -- the inference that he's urging you to adopt is not a sound one. And furthermore, I think that any doubts in that regard -- any doubts in that regard should be drawn in favour of the appellant. He has never had the opportunity to testify to you about these orders. He chose to testify at his trial below. Because he's not to have a new trial, per your decision, he'll never have the chance to testify about these orders, we'll never have the chance to question other witnesses at the trial about them. And quite frankly, I'm very troubled by the notion that you could find the evidence below deficient but then rely on new evidence that was not tested in the way that a trial tests evidence, and substitute in the new evidence and say: Well, the conviction is okay. I think that might trouble all of us. Further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, Judge Guney would like to put to you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hayman, the combat order that we have on our screens, was it signed by Colonel Blaskic? The combat order which is 93, 93. We have it on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is PA7, I believe, and on the -- I have the Croatian version in front of me. And it appears to be signed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the fourth paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Wait, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I may be looking at the wrong one. This is not the one I had. Which is this? PA12, I'm sorry. PA12 also appears to be signed in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: It was signed by the appellant?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It appears to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Now, in paragraph 4, and I quote: "I find Mr. Ljubicic personally responsible for effecting this task and preparation of the unit." [Interpretation] Within the frameworks of effective control, I would like to have your reactions, please, to this. How do you interpret things, as they stand? Somebody who could issue an order of this kind, did he actually have effective control?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Appellant was given, on the 15th, by the powers that be in Mostar, the ability to attach the military police to his command in the case of an all-out attack by the BH army forces. This order, PA12, was issued prior to that attachment. It is an order that relates to policing activities, the securing of the road. It -- he had the ability to do that, because under the rules of the military police administration, he could use the military police for policing. And it was only until there was a general conflict between the two armies, the next day, that the actual attachment would have taken effect, and at that point he would have had the additional authority, de jure authority, to order the military police to take a combat measure. That is the de jure picture. The de facto picture is totally different. You have heard from multiple witnesses, you have seen from many exhibits, that the principal person who could control and exercised effective control over the military police, the Jokers, and Pasko Ljubicic, was Dario Kordic. And our position is that because Dario Kordic had that ability to exercise effective control, that when the military police and the Jokers, when they commit a crime, when they go do something, it was incumbent on the Trial Chamber to look at the facts and circumstances and specifically analyse: Is this something that was ordered by Blaskic, because he controlled them at this time? Was this something that was ordered by Kordic, because he controlled them at this time? Or indeed, with respect to some of these units, were they committing criminal acts, looting, stealing, for their own personal gains at certain points in time? So that's the inquiry, that's the framework that we submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. I think it's time to break now. We resume at 12.35, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please be seated. So we resume the hearing with the submissions of the appellant in reply. Mr. Hayman, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, I did bring copies today -- excuse me. I did bring copies today of what we showed on the monitors yesterday, and I don't -- I'm not suggesting that any of that be evidence, but I'd like to lodge it so that at least it's in the record, because there will be portions in the transcript where we'll be referring to something, and unless that document is at least lodged in the record are, the transcript will be difficult to follow. So with your leave, I'd like to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll provide that to the staff. There's one more item I'd like to touch upon with respect to these four orders or reports that Mr. Farrell referenced this morning, PA7, 8, 9, 10, I believe they are, and that is the use of the term "our forces." Because the Prosecutor is arguing that our forces in the context of these orders means the Vitez Brigade, not our forces, Croatian forces. I invite you to look at the many other military documents in this case, HVO and BH army, and I'm going to show you one now, which is the 12th exhibit to the fourth Rule 115 motion, which is a BH army report. If you look at your computer evidence button, throughout this document, other documents, clearly, our forces is a common term used by both militaries in this culture to refer to the forces of our side. This particular report and this paragraph is referencing sending the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade to Ahmici to assist our forces. The Prosecutor does not maintain that as of the 16th of April, the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was already in Ahmici. They were not. And we're not suggesting they were already there either. Our forces is a commonly used term to refer to forces on the same side. So PA6, 7, 8, and so forth do not support the inference that counsel for the Prosecutor is suggesting. Now I'd like to go to PA38, which is a request on the 22nd of June from Colonel Blaskic to the Ministry of Defence, asking them to delay, for about a month, the dissolution of the Vitezovi because of urgent military circumstances. And he did do that. This report contains that request. And if we can find the one month and make sure that is visible, I would be grateful. You can work on that, perhaps. One month. There's a delay. Andrew, there's a phrase where he says: I believe it's necessary to delay this dissolution and reorganisation of the group for about a month. Which given the encirclement and the possible collapse of the Vitez-Busovaca enclave, is not -- is not unreasonable, it's not surprising, and this is a new exhibit. If the Prosecutor is suggesting that this order gives rise to failure to prevent liability, I pose the question: What crime? What crime did the Vitezovi commit after the 22nd of June, 1993? What did Colonel Blaskic fail to prevent by asking for a delay of one month? Let's think about that. Well, there are no charged crimes by the Vitezovi after the 22nd of June. It is true the judgement convicted the appellant for the Vitezovi's attack on Stari Vitez on the 18th of July. That was not charged in the indictment. There's a charge of an attack on Stari Vitez in August of 1993, no proof was ever produced of that claim. There's no attack in July of 1993 charged in the indictment on Stari Vitez. Another example of us trying to figure out what we're defending against at trial. So I submit, number one, the conviction for the Stari Vitez July incident must be reversed anyway, because it was not properly charged; but number two, you have now heard the testimony, the clear testimony, of BA5, to the effect there were no civilian deaths in the 18 July 1993 military fiasco, by the way, and it was a fiasco, 26 HVO dead, they were apparently marching across an open field towards Vitez and they were just mowed down. Not an attack that had any indicia of a professional military combat operation, I note which was I think commented on in the evidence. But BA5 said no civilian deaths, no significant civilian casualties as a result of that. So we don't believe there was a crime on the 18th of July. We don't believe any crime was charged, and in any event, we think -- and that is our analysis of PA38. Now I'd like to go to PA41. This is very interesting, and is again an example of I really -- I believe counsel, vigorous counsel, doing their best to present the evidence to Your Honours, but this evidence has been mispresented to Your Honours. There are two documents in this case which are SIS reports, but they are not from SIS Vitez, which was Sliskovic, or SIS Mostar. They're from the Vitez centre, SIS Vitez centre. What was the SIS centre in Vitez? The testimony in the case was that another group affiliated with Kraljevic of the Vitezovi set up their own intelligence centre in Vitez; indeed, Kraljevic appointed himself the deputy chief of the Vitez SIS centre. And if you look at PA41 and PA3, which we're going to look at in a moment, these are documents from Kraljevic's SIS centre in Vitez. How do we know this? If this is PA41, first I'd like to blow up the top. Good. Travnik Vitez centre. This is unlike any other logo letterhead that you will see on any SIS reports. For example, there's a SIS -- strike that. For example, compare with D608. It's under seal. I'm not going to say anything more about it. Compare this letterhead with the letterhead on Defence Exhibit D608 and you will see the distinction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There's one other of these documents. It's PA3. So now we're going to blow up again the letterhead, so you can see that once again it's this SIS centre Travnik/Vitez. And then at the end of this document, there's another tell-tale clue that this is a Kraljevic document. Look who signed this document. Godfather. That is Kraljevic. That is one of his aka's, consistent with his modus operandi. So -- and how -- why else do you know this? Why else should you infer this? PA41 gives a description of the Kalen gas station incident, which is totally inconsistent with all the other documents in the case. We have in the other documents Blaskic writing to Mostar, complaining that the Vitezovi have taken over the gas station. We have a reply from Mostar, again saying Vitezovi, you're subordinated, you know, do what you're told, whatever. And then we have this outlier document, PA41, which is a totally inconsistent version of events, highly favourable to Kraljevic, written or controlled by Kraljevic. And then similarly, if you look at PA3 -- why don't we go to that? That's the second document that is authored by this SIS Vitez centre. If you look at it, what this document basically talks about is that there's this horrible clique in and around Vitez that is portrayed negatively, and everyone's in it except for Kraljevic. And that is why Blaskic is lumped in with the Kordic Busovaca group, because Kraljevic was no friend of Blaskic's. You've heard that indeed, at one point, Kraljevic tried to liquidate or kill Colonel Blaskic. That's in the SIS reports, the true Mostar SIS reports, et cetera. So PA41 and PA3 are two very tricky documents. They purport to be bona fide SIS documents. They're actually documents from a SIS centre in Vitez that was controlled by Kraljevic. Indeed, he was the deputy of that centre. Now I'm going to go to the term "mop-up," which we've spent a fair amount of time on in the last few weeks. I have two further comments on this. One is: My learned opponent said this morning that the order D300, which is one of the orders to attack in Kiseljak, that it "left the door open to them, the forces in Kiseljak, to carry out ethnic cleansing operations." I don't know what that means. I don't know what standard that's referring to. If you give someone a gun and you tell them they're a soldier, are you leaving the door open to them for carrying out ethnic cleansing operations? If you look at D299 and D300 in conjunction with the war diary, I really -- I ask Your Honours: What else could Blaskic have done to give more specific directions to those units in Kiseljak to stay out of the villages and to pursue the military targets, the high ground? I submit there is nothing else he could have done. He pursued that very diligently. My second point on mop-up is the Prosecutor relies on Brian Watters' testimony, something to the effect that there was ethnic cleansing in Kiseljak and it may have been described as a mopping-up operation. This issue of the term "mop-up" was not an issue in the trial. It was not litigated. It was not scrutinised with one per cent of the scrutiny that it has been given the last two weeks or ten days. So my point there is: Watters was not shown, to my recollection, any of the relevant orders. He was not asked about the use of the term "mop-up," he was not asked about the context in which that term was used in the relevant orders. This comment was an aside, and without any context, without being shown an order by Colonel Blaskic, and that is all it is. It was a side comment. And make no mistake: We are not suggesting that the term "mop-up" could never be used to imply ethnic cleansing. In the context, in a particular context, it might well be capable of being used, but what we know from the testimony here, the expert testimony and the rigorous review of the actual orders in the case, as well as comparison with other documents in the case, that Colonel Blaskic, in all of these documents, and in the war diary, used "mop-up" with its strict military usage. And Mr. Nobilo pointed that out, I thought very well yesterday, within he pointed out the war diary section that said: Don't engage in mop-up. You will have too many casualties. Clearly a reference to military -- eliminating military pockets of resistance. One moment, Your Honour. I'm checking my notes for missed items. There was a reference to a report on or about May 9th that Colonel Blaskic sent to the HVO in Mostar, talking about a number of things, but including references to Ahmici. And he does express in that report concern that the media is focussing exclusively on Ahmici and not providing any coverage of crimes against Croats in the Lasva Valley. And indeed, there had been crimes. There are cases charged before this Tribunal, the Lasva Dusina massacre, et cetera, where Croats were massacred, and the media simply hadn't picked up on it. And I would ask you to understand the frustration that a commander could have at that situation, which is very different from any motive or desire to cover up or not see through to the end of a thorough investigation and Prosecution a massacre like the massacre in Ahmici. And I also note: In that report, Colonel Blaskic wrote: Mate Boban should have been here in Vitez today, which I submit is a reference to: He should be here. He should be here to see these things himself. Mate Boban was the president of Herceg-Bosna, the Herzegovinian-based political entity. So, I think if you look at Colonel Blaskic's statement at the press conference, the read on his mental state by Colonel Stewart that he was horrified on the 22nd of April, when he learned about Ahmici, the fact that he did not tell Colonel Duncan on the 9th of May that Ahmici was some kind of a Serb attack; in that context, if you look at this report, this communication to Mostar, these are consistent. They are consistent messages; they reflect a consistent mens rea state, and one which is radically different from the mens rea state that the Prosecution has gone to great lengths to try and depict in this case. I'd like to say a short word about persecution, which was commented on by one of the counsel this morning. Persecution is a specific intent crime, as described in the Krnojelac appellate decision, and indeed an accused must intend each and every underlying act. Persecution is second in gravity and severity only to genocide. There is still in this case no evidence of discriminatory intent. Counsel spoke this morning of the appellant's discriminatory actions speak louder than his words. What actions? What did he do? We're still, seven years later -- what exactly did he do? We have his orders now. What is it that he did that the Prosecutor maintains is discriminatory? He gave orders that Muslims were in the to be removed from their homes, he gave orders that homes were not to be burned, he gave an order on April 18th, 1993, within 48 hours of the general conflict, that all detainees should be released. Do those orders evince a discriminatory intent or animus, or do they evince something else? That is, a military commander, a young military commander with the training of the rank of captain in the JNA trying to do things by the book, writing orders, expecting them to be obeyed, when in reality, the people that perhaps had the most control in the situation were the mafia-type figures, who had local connections, local control, or were the kind of brazen people, like Rajic in Kiseljak, or Kraljevic in the Vitezovi, who would pull out their side arm and put it up against the head of another in order to force their will. The appellant was not that kind of person. Every witness to testify in this case that has commented on the subject has testified to an absence of any animus or ethnic bias on the part of the appellant. According to the Prosecutor, that was all staged. He was just very careful what he said, for years on end, and it was a trick. You're professional Judges. We submit it to you for your evaluation. We've already spoken of the Duncan error with respect to the May 9th meeting. We've already spoken of the Danas interview, written interview. I want to turn now briefly to the issue of orders, and the ambiguity in the Prosecutor's positions with respect to how Your Honours should evaluate the orders of the accused. At times, they have suggested they were sham orders. At times they have suggested that the humanitarian orders he issued should not be given any weight because they were issued after events, or after complaints, and thus they weren't true preventative orders. That seems to us to be -- we have two responses to that. One is, I'm going to go through -- well, we've already gone through orders that predated the April conflict, but that is the first point. There were a number of orders that predated the general conflict and the commission of crimes in April. If those aren't preventative, then we don't know how the Prosecutor defines preventative. But furthermore, when a crime was committed, when a house was burned but no perpetrator is identified, and Colonel Blaskic issued an order compelling the removal of criminal elements from units or ordering that any such activity immediately cease, et cetera, the Prosecutor takes the position: Well, that's not a preventative order. What would they have had him do? We submit, if he had not issued these orders to try and curtail all such misconduct, you would of course be hearing about that now, that a failure to act would be a failure to prevent further misconduct. So we have some of the humanitarian orders that he issued displayed here. We have a great deal more of them set forth at pages 38 and 40 of our brief. These particular orders deal with detainees, and there are similar lists and recitations of orders in evidence that relate to the protection of civilian property, the protection of civilians, and so forth. I also note the suggestion -- and they don't come out and make the argument, but the suggestion that these are all sham orders is illogical, given that, one, the Trial Chamber never made a finding that appellant's orders were sham orders; and two, these orders, with one exception, which I'll comment on, these orders were marked confidential, military secret. They went nowhere but the file and to the units, and then were disseminated downward. They were not mailed out on the front of the command or sent to CNN or the ICRC and so forth. Now, there is one order that you saw during the hearing last week, which was actually in English, was prepared and signed by the appellant, which, quite plainly -- and then it was directed to BritBat and ECMM, because that was an order specifically in light of what had occurred prior to that date that appellant wanted to get that order in the pocket of every EC monitor and every UN personnel so if they encountered a problem in the field they could pull out Blaskic's signed order, and in essence, help spread the word. But with the exception of that one order, all these orders were sent to the troops. They weren't sent to the media, they weren't sent to international humanitarian organisations. And that was part of the problem. You heard from the Prosecutor this morning that read a portion of Colonel Stewart's statement at trial. Colonel Stewart testified that he's sure, he was sure Colonel Blaskic was horrified by the crime in Ahmici, but Colonel Stewart became dissatisfied with the lack of progress on the part of Colonel Blaskic in bringing anyone to justice for the Ahmici crime. Why would Colonel Stewart have been dissatisfied with that process? He didn't have any information about it. These were internal processes. The orders to SIS to investigate, the Sliskovic report, the other documents, they were internal, confidential, military documents, and they would be in any army. As Watkins told you, we should not expect Colonel Blaskic or any other professional military officer to air their dirty laundry with international observers. And if Colonel Blaskic had had a more effective public relations or information and propaganda department, if he had had some professionals in that area, they might have done better, I'm sure they would have, at educating the international organisations that were on the ground with respect to what was going on, what was being done to try and maintain control, protect civilians, investigate the Ahmici case, and so forth. Now, I want to comment briefly on one of these orders, a different type of order, PA52. PA52 is the -- this is a Prosecution document, and it talks about not allowing the representatives of the Red Cross to visit facilities other than official detention, et cetera. You have this document. It's in evidence. And what I'm concerned about is that at the 11th hour, in the form of this rebuttal evidence, you see a handful, a couple of orders that appear to be inconsistent and out of character with everything else that you see from Colonel Blaskic. And there are only a couple of them, and -- I'm getting French on channel 4. Perhaps I'm being punished for my earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Everybody has been shifted to the French translation, actually. Technical problem. Are we having now the English on channel 4? Can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Shall we test it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I hear only English now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I was speaking of PA52, and the concern here is we have an order such as this that comes in in rebuttal, and there's no testimony about it. There's in explanation. The appellant will never have the opportunity to comment and give testimony on this. It says: Don't allow the representatives of the Red Cross to visit facilities other than official detentions, and do not admit that there are any other detainees anywhere else. We don't know what the background here is. We don't know. We do know that there are a number of other orders, including on 29 April, within 48 hours of this order, Colonel Blaskic issued an order to all brigades - and this is Defence Exhibit 366 - to identify and release all detainees and to cooperate with the Red Cross in this process. What I would note with respect to this order, PA52, is there has never been a claim that detainees were concealed from the Red Cross, there's never been a claim that the Red Cross was denied access to any detention centre, never been charged, no proof, no argument. So why is PA52 here? One could speculate, and we're not trying to withdraw it from evidence. It's in evidence. You have it, and you absolutely should consider it. But we submit that we don't have enough information for this to be a meaningful document. And in any event, whatever it is, it appears to relate to something that has never been charged as a crime in this case, and there's no evidence that any crime was committed, because, as I said, there's no evidence that any detainee was ever concealed or that the Red Cross was ever denied access to any detainee. Similarly, Exhibit 56 is another late-coming document to this case, which is the document in which the third paragraph was crossed out by the appellant. It's a warning relating to the death -- the deaths of MOS members, that someone has been killed by a sniper while digging trenches at our defence lines. And again, we don't know more about this document than the face of the document. We know that the appellant did not agree with the third paragraph, which he crossed out. We know he didn't draft the document. If you look at the initials in the lower left-hand corner, he was not the author of the document. And we know that the appellant issued numerous orders concerning the proper treatment of detainees, both before and after PA56. Defence Exhibit 373 is an order on the 21st of June, which, among other things, forbids the uses of prisoners of war for coerced engineering projects on the territory. And I note that the evidence in the case with respect to work platoons is that work platoons were organised to prepare defensive lines, not on front-line locations. That's Prosecutor's Exhibits 715 to 717. And that those work platoons were composed of Croats, Muslims, Serbs, and gypsies. Work platoons were part of the law of the former Yugoslavia. You were conscripted, you either fought in the armed forces or you worked in a work platoon. So that is the context for that issue. And with respect to the Red Cross access issue, we have a number of exhibits in evidence. Here is a list of some of them. Granting access to international organisations, 16 January, 27 January, 13 February, 21 April. And these orders are entirely consistent with the testimony of Mr. Watkins that he got access when he needed it, and he got it through Colonel Blaskic, who helped him get access for international organisations to where they needed to be. And on this second slide, there are five additional humanitarian orders. If I could take a brief moment to confer with co-counsel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours weren't at the trial, and -- do we have audio? Do we have audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Q. In your meetings and conversations with Colonel Blaskic, did he ever threaten any harm towards ECMM, BritBat or any other international organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact he cooperated with ECMM, wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seemed so. Whenever we had a request, he tried to come forward to us and assist him." That was Mr. Friis-Pedersen, 16 December 1997 at 5510.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Q. Did Colonel Blaskic express any ethnic animosity towards any ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think that he was saying to me that he felt that people ought to be able to live together."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was Charles McLeod, author of the report on interethnic violence, 28 January, 1998, at 6445.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Q. You said that Mr. Valenta expressed views which could be described as being in favour of ethnic division; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever hear or hear of Tihomir Blaskic expressing any such views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was Roy Hunter, 11 December 1997 at 5125.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Q. In fact, is it fair to say that Colonel Blaskic never in any conversation with you spoke of Muslims with racial prejudice in his statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was -- that's correct, yes, that's correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was Alastair Duncan, 3 June 1998, at 9172.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Q. Were you ever told that Colonel Blaskic had made any inflammatory or ethnically prejudicial or derogatory remarks on TV, radio, in speeches or otherwise, during your tour of duty? Did you ever receive such information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was Henrik Morsink, 2 July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Q. [Interpretation] Tihomir Blaskic ever speak against the Muslim as a people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was Fuad Zeco, 26 September, 1997. One more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "A. [Interpretation] I never heard Mr. Blaskic say anything bad about any nationality, or that he would give bad names to other -- members of other ethnic groups. I never heard him do anything of that kind."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Ivica Pervan, 3 November 1998. Your Honours, based on all of the evidence in the record, we believe that no reasonable tribunal of fact could have convicted appellant of the crimes charged. We ask you to acquit him, based on the totality of the record. We thank you for your efforts on this case. I'd also like to thank the staff, the technical staff, the staff of the Registrar's Office that have been extraordinarily helpful to our being able to participate effectively, and indeed, they are a symbol of the fairness and the justice that we find in this institution. With that, we conclude our argument. The appellant would like to make a brief statement when convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Hayman. May I first turn to my colleagues, if they want to put any question to the Defence. So that is not the case. We still have on our agenda the item of a personal address of General Blaskic to the Court. Before turning to this, I would like to thank both parties for their very professional arguments. We are here to do justice, and both the Prosecution and the Defence have greatly assisted the Bench. I say that on behalf of the entire Bench. This is a very complex case that has lasted a long time, both at the trial and at the appeal stage. It is therefore also important that we have had very professional assistance from both sides, Defence and Prosecution. Now, General Blaskic, would you rise, please. Should you wish so, would you like to address the Court briefly, General? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Mr. President. Your Honours, I should like to thank you for giving me this opportunity to address you, and I should like to express my regrets for all the casualties of this war, particularly the Muslim Bosniak casualties, who lost their lives through the acts of individuals and members and groups of the Croatian Defence Council. Those members of the Croatian Defence Council who perpetrated crimes have put shame on our army and the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to which I myself belong to that people. They have thrown shame on all honourable defenders, those who defended their country, their homeland, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I never ordered a single crime to be committed, and I did everything in my power to prevent any crimes from being committed and to clear up the units of the Croatian Defence Council from the criminals. I am very sorry that in the event of a war, and during those critical years, I did not have more power, a better-organised army, to prevent the crimes which unfortunately occurred in Central Bosnia. Although I am conscious of the fact that within the frameworks of my limited possibilities, I did try to prevent violence towards civilians, I am also conscious that in addition to that, too much violence was done. When the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia began, I left the Yugoslav People's Army and went to Austria, intending to start a peaceful life there. However, once my homeland, Bosnia-Herzegovina, was jeopardised by the Montenegrin Serbian aggression, and especially my local community in Kiseljak, which was attacked, I felt it my duty to accept the call by the leadership of the Kiseljak municipality, which was populated by Bosnian Muslim and Croatian people, and to help them to come to their assistance in the defence and in the organisation of military units there. I was born in the region. My parents lived in the region, and all my relatives did too. When I became the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, I was 32 years old, and my last post in the Yugoslav People's Army was deputy commander of the battalion commander. And I had the rank of captain when I left the Yugoslav People's Army. Before taking on the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, I was not in command of a single unit greater than a company, that is to say, 100 to 120 soldiers. That was the full complement. The task to organise a Croatian Defence Council, with the necessary military control, was a very difficult task, and a very complex one as well, because what was needed was continuous defence operations and activities, and to use that same army to organise the overall military set-up. And I think that that was not fully -- that was not done even until the end of 1994. I believed in the establishment of a joint command with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that together we could defend Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Serb aggression. And never did it enter my mind that I would ever be placed in a situation where I would be fighting our allies, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To my great chagrin as a commander and as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina myself, because of the overall global policy that was being waged and the adverse events that took place during the war, tensions grew and burgeoned between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, and a military conflict broke out in 1993. When the civil war began between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council, I collaborated strongly with all representatives of the international community, and I told many of them that they were in fact our allies, for us, together with the BH army, to be able to establish a truce and to sign an agreement on a truce. However, as I was also a military commander in the midst of this conflict, it was my duty, and I also had the authority and competence, to order legal, lawful combat operations against the forces of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, which is what I did. Although I very much regret that the conflict ever took place, it was my duty, however, to protect the Croatian community in the enclaves, and all the population living in those isolated pockets throughout Central Bosnia. My lawyers have already explained why I am innocent, with respect to the indictment, and it is not intention to present all the arguments in my defence here and now. However, I should just like to mention Ahmici. I cannot but mention Ahmici. I did not plan anything, I did not order anything, nor did I in any way take part in the commission of crimes in Ahmici. I hope that this is quite clear, after my own testimony and after all the new documents that were presented here in Court and that were accepted within the appeals process and after the new witnesses that we heard testimony from in the past few days. The orders that I issued on the 15th and 16th of April, 1993 have nothing to do with the crimes perpetrated on that same day. I issued the orders for my -- because of my justified fears, that the HVO in Central Bosnia would be attacked and that it would be routed, destroyed, especially in Vitez, where the situation seemed without any exit. When Colonel Stewart, from UNPROFOR, provided me with the information about the crimes in Ahmici, I was deeply shocked and upset, and the true scope of the crimes I got to know only here during my trial. I called a meeting of the commanders of the operative zone when I heard about it. I read Colonel Stewart's letter out and I demanded SIS to conduct an investigation therein. I asked assistance from Colonel Stewart as well. I did so in writing. The next day I sent him that letter, asking for assistance, and several days later, once I had toured Ahmici, at a press conference for domestic and foreign journalists, including the BBC and the reporter Martin Bell, and also some representatives of UNPROFOR, I was the first Croat who said that what happened in Ahmici was a horrendous crime. I condemn the crime, and I stressed that I would demand an investigation to be undertaken. I also stressed that nothing like that should ever be repeated again. And I still consider that I did everything in my power to implement an investigation of that kind, because I knew that the members of the military police were in Ahmici. I asked SIS to conduct that investigation, because SIS was the sole competent authority to conduct an investigation of the military police. As we have heard so many times today, and in the previous days, about the interview that appeared in the weekly Danas, I feel that I have to mention it myself. As I've already explained during the course of my testimony at trial, I never talked to that journalist in actual fact. The interview took the form of a list of written questions which was faxed to the headquarters of the operative zone in Vitez, and my assistant wrote out an answer, a response to those questions. I failed to control the answers and responses made to those questions, or that list of questions, and I came to understand that that was a mistake, allowing the article to come out in print without my authorisation, and I am ashamed that members of my headquarters were able to lie like that and that that kind of article was ever allowed to appear in print. However, I should like to stress that the interview does not express my stands and positions with respect to the crimes and that I presented my positions both at a press conference, and that Colonel Stewart and Martin Bell and all the rest of them who were present at that press conference were able to hear my positions. When the crimes in Ahmici were committed, I realised that I had to do everything in my power to conduct an investigation to prevent a repetition of crimes like that, and in that respect, I issued a series of humanitarian orders to ensure the application of humanitarian law, international humanitarian law, and I tried to set up and organise the army, to organise it better and to increase discipline in the army and within the units of the Croatian Defence Council. At the same time, I did my best to get authorisation from my superiors to place the military police under my control, so as to make it an instrument of justice and the law instead of a weapon in the hands of those who exerted violence, especially towards the Bosniak Muslims. As you have learnt throughout this trial, I have -- I did try to replace and succeeded in replacing the command of the military police, and later on to reorganise and restructure the entire military police force, and I personally endeavoured to organise training, although I had no military police knowledge beforehand, because I was never an officer of the military police myself. I hope that thus far you have been able to understand the very difficult tasks that stood before me and how difficult it was to command forces of the HVO faced with a complete encirclement and siege in 1993, militarily speaking. And I'm militarily convinced that every soldier would say what Colonel Stewart told me before he left, that I was in a situation in which it was difficult to find a way out, a situation in the Vitez pocket in which the people and the army would be routed and destroyed. It was also impossible to control the forces and leaders in the enclave who had their own plans. You have heard here in the courtroom about the differences between my own positions and those of the extremist political leaders in Central Bosnia, their positions. Perhaps you're wondering and asking yourselves how I could have met with them and worked with leaders of that kind. I should like to tell you that I was a professional soldier and that I considered it to be my -- that my mission was a military mission, exclusively. I did send out reports to the political leaders of the community of Herceg-Bosna, and when I was assigned a military task, I endeavoured to find the best way of carrying it out. But first of all, a military one and a lawful and legal one, to put it into effect. I did not know about the criminal military operations, and I never carried them out myself. The positions of the extreme nationalists were ones that I never shared myself, nor did they influence me in any way, myself as a soldier, and I did everything I could to protect the entire population within the enclave, while also leading the HVO in that difficult year of 1993. Perhaps I should have made more public statements and stood up against the positions of the leaders, the political leaders, but that was contrary to my professional code of conduct, as an officer, to criticise political leaders vis-a-vis third parties. That is something that I myself never did. Instead of that, I thought that it was my duty to reform the Croatian Defence Council, to organise it and structurise it better, and that I myself could deal with the dirty linen that existed in my own house. Although I wasn't able to prevent all the crimes, we did succeed in defending the enclave successfully, and also to prevent violence, so that after Ahmici, there were no similar crimes that were committed. So I am proud of that success, just as I am that we managed to defend ourselves within the enclave. In the second half of 1993, I almost wholly succeeded in establishing control and discipline and to make it impossible for any violence to be exerted towards the Bosniak Muslims. The question was often raised in court why I didn't resign. That was a question I was asked. I am fully conscious that resignation for me, after Ahmici, perhaps would have been a way out. Perhaps I would never have been brought before this Tribunal and accused. However, had I resigned, faced in a situation of siege and encirclement, when the ratio of forces was 1 to 10 to 12 to the advantage of the BH army, without an experienced military personnel to take over the defence of the enclave, there would have been a collapse in the military sense, and in the chaos that would have ensued, I'm quite convinced that there would have been far greater violence towards the civilians on all sides and against all sides. Perhaps the times and my concept of military duty, the duty of an officer, played me a fool, but I am sure that I never dishonoured my soldiers or the population of the enclave. I am proud that although the Prosecution erroneously claimed for seven years, alleged for seven years, that I ordered killings and the other sufferings of the Muslim civilians, not a single witness of the 164 testimonies that we heard here in this courtroom ever said that I had any prejudice or animosity or bias against the Bosniak Muslims, nor did a single individual state that they had ever heard or that they had seen me issue orders along those lines. I should like to be able to explain to you how painful it all was, how difficult it all was. It was difficult for my family and myself when I was convicted of crimes which I did not order, nor did I commit. Above all, I wish to express my regret for all the casualties of the crimes and all those who were killed during the war in Central Bosnia, and I would like to express my condolences to the victims' families. I should like to say that it would be a wonderful thing had there never been a conflict between the Bosniaks and Croats and that the civil war which cost us so many lives had never, ever been waged to begin with. However, my conscience is clear, because I know from my heart that I wholeheartedly did everything to prevent crimes and to conduct an investigation into the crimes as soon as I learnt of them. I should like especially to thank all the witnesses who came forward to testify and thus helped this Honourable Tribunal to establish the truth. I am convinced that everybody's good intents and evil intents and actions will ultimately be made known. Nothing more remains for me, Your Honours, than to hope that you will carefully consider all the evidence placed before you, that you will look at my role objectively in all the events that came to pass, as well as the actual command responsibility that I had, how much I was able to command at all, and that you will make the right decision, the right judgement, based on evidence and proof, and that will be a true contribution to a sure and certain future to the population in Central Bosnia, and I hope that people will extend hands of friendship to each other for total reconciliation and trust and confidence. The Prosecution, on one occasion, said, in this courtroom, that the dead deserve the truth, and that is very true. The dead do deserve the truth. But the living also deserve the truth and deserve justice. I am deeply convinced that your decisions and judgement will do both: They will assure the truth and justice. Your Honours, I should like to thank you for your patience and understanding during the presentation of evidence and for the time you have accorded me to say these final words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, General Blaskic. You may sit down. Now our hearing in this appeal comes to an end. I want to thank everybody again. We will now rise. The judgement will be rendered in due course. The hearing stands adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.38 p.m.
